Widnes Corporation's Enterprise. At the Widnes Corporation Gas Works on Tuesday IL gigantic carbonising plant was in- stalled. This makes possible a further reduc- tion in the price of gas. The Widnes charges for gas are the lowest in the country, being now 27 per cent. below those of Sheffield, the nearest competitor. The formal opening ceremony was performed by Mrs. IL Sutton Timmis, wife of Alderman H. S. Timmis, who .as been chair- man of the Gas Committee for twenty-two years. Mrs. Timmis was presented with a hand- some silver rose bowl bearing the inscription: "Presented to Mrs. H. S. Timmis. Inaugura- tion of new Gas Works, June 23. 1914, by the Gas and Water Committee"; and Mr. Timmis was also presented, on behalf of Messrs. Drakes, Limited, the contractors, with a gold cigar- ease.

After these ceremonies the company inspected the modernised system ,of mechanical charging and discharging in the retort-house. div.head: TONING BROMIDE PRINTS.
div.p: TONING BROMIDE PRINTS.

The most common source of failure in sul- i'Ae toning has been its liability to produce yellow tones, even from strong originals. • is would occur without warning when every u 'c-caution had been taken in development, fix- sag, washing, ST. For a long time no satisfac- tory explanation was forthcoming, but experi- ment has proved that tire trouble is due to the 1 uastable nature of sodium sulphide. It is very dcult ,to obtain this salt in a pure state, and when so obtained it is practically impossible to IczYep it pure, even by the exercise of extreme cy:a. Whether in crystal, in solution, or in any 01,.r form it tends to decompose, and to be- come partly converted into hypo. Now the 1.-±sult or applying a solution of hypo to a b'eached print is that a part, .at least, of the 01-iginal silver image is dissolved away, and the r:Niulting tone, instead of being a strong, rich • is a weak, yellowish colour. Certain c: Japounds of sodium, tin and sulphur, how- • have, been found to be free from this tadency to become converted into hypo, and will sulphide a bleached image in the same way as the unstable sodium salt. The application off these compounds to photography is quite novel, and has been protected by the discoverers —Barrougties. Wellcome and Co. A suitable cvabination is presented as "Tabloid and Sul- Liding Compound." It produces rich, per- -ru,nent sepia tones on bromide and gaslight •;nts, and can also be used successfully for tcaing lantern slides and transparencies.

div.head: PHOTOGRAPHY.
div.p: PHOTOGRAPHY.
CONFERENCE ON ORGANISED CHARITIES.
PHILANTHROPIC SOCIETIES MEET.

Recently Newcastle was the gathering place of various philanthropic societies. The Guilds of Help had on this occasion joined hands with the Charity Organisation Societies and Councils ofSocial Welfare. The joint meetings brought together delegates from Scotland and Ireland, as well as from England and Wales. The proceed- ings opened wifli n receptiah by the Lord Mayor, who 'was accompanied b'y 'one of the most im- pressive mayor-bearers in the country'. :There was an excellent muslcal programme. The chief speakers were Mr. Woollcomhe, of the recently- formed Cavendish Association', and 'Principal Hadow, of Armstrong College, who made a most witty speech.

The Law and the Family. The whole of Tuesday ..morning was devoted to serious confereneeFirst came a paper on "Law in relation to the family." It had been written bY Mr. Lillyard; the man who started the .institution known as the Poor Man's Lawyer. In his absence the pa'per was read by Mr. Wrigley; who acts as ,a poor man's lawyer in Manchester. The discussion was opened in a singularly able speech by Dr. Ethel Williams. well known for her report to the Poor Law 'Com- mission on the condition of. widows and children in receipt of out-relief. The points chiefly dis- cussed were payments under separation and affiliation orders. It was quite evident that the general desire among these experienced social workers was that such payments ought to be made through police courts. _
The Sheriff of Newcastle presided for the ,first half of the morning, and then gave place to Sir Thomas Oliver.

Continued Need for Philanthropy. The second paper was concerned with "The effects of the Insurance Act on organised volun- tary work." Certain speakers were disposed to think that some part of the financial burden had been taken from the shoulders of the phil- anthropic public: Others pointed out that tilos.? who formerly relied upon poor law assistance now looked to charities to supplement sickness benefit derived from the Insurance Act. But those with fullest knowledge deprecated the passing of any final judgment on the effects of this law until a much wider experience of its working had been gained. The general con- census of opinion was that organised ,philan- thropies were more necessary than ever to co- ordinate legislative and other efforts for human betterment. A good deal of attention was devoted to the onestion of Tuberculosis and After Care—a sub- ject in which the Warrington Guild has taken a deep interest. On Tuesday afternoon delegates had a wide choice before them. Arrangements had .been made to visit a home for the feeble-minded at Jarrow; to inspect a shipyard and see a launch; to steam down the Tyne; or to visit places of antiquarian interest in the city. On returning from one or other of these excursions, the Guilds of Help went to one centre and the Charity Organisation Societies to another, each section; conducting a meeting for queAtions and answers on points arising out of charity administration.

Need for Voluntary Work. There was a good public meeting in the even- ing on the subject of " National Demands for Voluntary Work." This was arranged by the Guilds, while the Charity Organisation Socie- ties made plans for the following evening. Wednesday morning was given up to separ- ate business sessions of the different bodies. The most delightful experience came on the Wednes- day afternoon, when bright sunshine succeeded the incessant heavy rains of the previous day. A special excursion train ran out past Ifealiam to the wonderful Roman remains at Chesters on the North Tyne. About 300 visitors were received at the private estate which contains a wealth of Roman relics. both in the museum and in early traced ruins. The whole situa- tion was most picturesque and delegates ad- mired the gardens, the handsome house and its famous pictures.

Experiment Justified. The experiment of bringing together the various societies with common aims was frillv justified. There was evidence of mutual good- will, which in future years may beer fruit in some working understanding. But there is no immediate prospect of either section sacrificing its individuality, and next year separate con- ferences will be held, though it is hoped that joint meetings will be arranged at some future date.

div.head: LOVELY LANE SCHOOL
div.p: LOVELY LANE SCHOOL
Why it is to be Built Near the Railway. A "LOP-SIDED" BUILDING.

At a meeting of the Pducation Committee on Monday evening the Sites and Buildings Com- mittee recommended: "That Messrs. Wright and Hamlyn be appointed the architects for the Lovely-lane Council School upon the terms and conditions set forth in the— conditions of competition; and that Mr. W. Davenport be appointed to prepare the•-necessary quantities at an inclusive fee at the rate of 11 per cent." -Mr. R. T. FAIRCLOUGH moved, and Mr. G. WALKER seconded, the confirmation of the min- utes. Mr. JARMAN asked if it was the usual thing for someone else to prepare quantities, instead of the architect? Mr. tesos safil he had only just seen the plan and noticed the schools would be "101-sided." Was it not possible, he asked, to get the other (Monk-street) corner' of the site, and also to have the schools away from the railway? Alderman BENNETT agreed with Mrs:. Upson, but said it was not the fault of the„architects, who had made very good use of the site: He had been laughed to scorn for wanting to make the school an object of beauty in the neighbour- hood; but it did seem to him they might boar that point in mind when securing other sites. The CHAIRMAN: The site was fixed for us by the General Purposes Committee, and `we had no voice in the matter. Alderman BmisETT : I admit that. The archi- tects were bound by the decision of the anti- quated General Purposes Committee, and it was not their fault. Councillor PEilmeßTox said it was the usual thing to have a quantities clerk; it was a great safeguard. Canon STEVENSON: It is terrible for teachers to be in schools near the railway, amj it-is Much to be regretted that: sites cannot be got else- where. - Councillor WILKINSON: I think tins matter was thrashed out—

PEMBERTON : No. Councillor WILKINSON: When will you be in harmony with anyone else? (Laughter). Of the two dangers we took the least, and we recommended the site nearer the railway in preference to one near the fever hospital. 7th. actual schoolrooms are brought as far from the railway as possible. FAIRCLOUGH : The site was fixed for us. and we were advised that it was better to have quantities clerk. The minutes were approved and adopted.

div.head: CURIOUS RUNCORN CASE.
div.p: CURIOUS RUNCORN CASE.

A curious point was decided at the uncorvl The Speed of a Heavy Motor. E, ' Petty Sessions on Monday. when the adjouei summons against Alfred Townson, for driving a heavy motor car at a speed ex- ceeding 12 miles per hour, on Whit Sunday. Was heard. • of Rishton, The Bench had heard arguments from Mr. Spafford, barrister, of Manchester, who-1-epre- seated the -defendant. Mr., Spafford contended that the information was wrong, and that ft ! motor car which paid hiickney •earriage duty in order that piissengers might be carried, for a profit, was entitled to the privileges of the triNV as applied to hackney ciarriages, and could there- fore travel at 20 miles an hour. The Chairman (Sir Frederick ;Norman.) said that the magistrates had had the opportunity of carefully considering the two points -oi law raised by Mr. Spafford. They had decided that the law was against him, and were now Prepared to hear evidence .as to the facts.. They were willing to state 'a ease if desired. Mr. Spaflord said there might be an appeal. After a lengthy hearing defendant was fined 40s. and costs.
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY,

div.head: WHAT THE COMMITTEE WILL DO AND
div.p: WHAT THE COMMITTEE WILL DO AND
WILL NOT DO.

The committee recommended That the Board of Education be informed that the proposals of the Governors of the Grammar School, as submitted to the Local Education Authority through the Board, have been carefully considered by the Local Educa- tion Authority, and that they have come to the following conclusions, viz.:— .‘

• (1) The proposal to provide a school for 200 scholars is too ambitious. There is no evidence that there is likely to be a demand for any- thing more than a very slight increase in the present number (117) of scholars.
, (2) The financial proposals of the governors require further consideration.

l 3) The Local Education Authority cannot give any guarantee to continue indefinitely the existing arrangement whereby- they are respon- sible for any deficit on the annual accounts for the maintenance of the school up to a sum of .elOO, for the following reasons, viz.: (a) The school, on account of its character, cannot be regarded as supplying the full educational needs of the area; and (b) the immediate pros- Rect of the Liwal Education Authority being called upon to provide further accommodation by means of a new girls' secondary school and the retention of a boys' secondary school in the existing Municipal Secondary School building. (4) Should the proposals of the Governors of the Grammar School be approved by the Board," and the erection of the new school be proceeded With, it must be distinctly understood that, in the event of the governors requiring the definite continuance of the present arrangement of mak- ing good any deficit up to X4OO, or an' further financial assistance from the Local Education Authority, this will only be considered on the basis of the municipalisation of the Grammar School. Canon STEVENSON moved the confirmation of the minutes, stating that he thought the minute set the matter forth quite explicitly, and he (lid not propose to say anything. He would, how- ever, answer any questions.

A WORD FOR THE SCHOOL AND THE GUARANTEE. Mr. C. S. Buttaess said he did not propose to enter into any discussion, at the present moment, of the policy of the School Manage- ment Committee, as set forth in their minutes. He thought, however, that the first resolution, which showed that the deficit to be made good last year was only £29 9s. id., was a striking comment on section 4 in the next resolution. Personally, he was, of course, very glad that the governors of the Grammar School did not re- quire more than £29 out of the £4OO which the comnaittee had guaranteed. He would like to say that, because he thought there was a wrong im- pression in that committee, and certainly in the town, as to the amount of support the Grammar School got from the local authoriff. It might be within their recollection that three months ago a prominent member of that committee made a statement to the effect that "he would not he afraid to meet his constituents in the ' town on the fact that they- were paying 355. per head for elementary education, and £1 per head for the Grammar School." That was a mistake. The average amount paid by that authority to the Grammar School was less than £2 per head, the average total deficiency made good being about £l6O per year. He did not think that was a large amount for what was obtained. As re- garded the proposals set forth ia the present scheme, it might be ambitious to build for 200 scholars, but the difference between building for 150 and 200 would be so slight that he thought etlz ger o:e-ernors would do better by building for 200. He did not think the governors or anyone thought that they provided the full educational needs of the area, but he did claim that they met a very special need, which would have to be provided for by somebody. If it had to be provided by that authority it would Probably cost the town £2,000 or £3,000. He did not think the time had arisen for discussion on section 4. It would be sufficiently early when the estimates had arrived. There was no doubt a very real, clear and straightforward agree- ment between the governors and the committee, and it was that the committee would guarantee to Pay any deficit in any one year up to £4O0— not more—on condition that the governors main- tained 16 Scholarships and granted ad- ilitionalthe Is,ecrhoolfarftieyspc places slts innotny : sontleia3n-ea2or per cent. of the whole attendance at the school.

div.head: CLASSES AND EDUCATION.
div.p: THE CLASSES AND EDUCATION.
Alderman Bennett says "Snobbish," But , _ _ Must Deal With Facts.

Alderman BENNETT said he felt very strongly on the matter, and he moved that the resolu- tion be not approved and adopted. The com- mittee objected to the governors' proposal primarily, because they thought the proposal to build a school for 200 boys was too ambitious. hut in view of what they said in the latter part of their recommendations, he should have thought it was not ambitions enough. They were not building, for to-day, nor to-morrow, hut for the future; and he was satisfied that the time was not far distant when every lad in the country, who had any capacity, would be edu- cated until. he was at least 16 years of age. At the present time we allowed a ridiculous mini- mum, which was too low. He did not see. why lads of /the rich should have those facilities and lads of the poor should not. (Hear, hear.) The second objection was as to the financial proposals, which were said to require further consideration. He had no doubt they would receive further consideration; blithe Wished to say that they were based on the figures and cal- culations of a gentleman who was recognised as one of the greatest of local financial authori- ties. Our Educational Edifice.

The School Management Committee, went on to say that no guarantze could be given because the character of the school could ..not be re-I garded as supplying the full educational *needs of the town. No one imagined for one moment that it would supply the full educational needs of the town, and certainly he did not, but it dia fill in one very important corner-stone in the edifice. (Hear, hear.) It was suggested that the Grammar School might be utilised for meet- ing the need for another Secondary School, but lie did not think that was the best solution. Ills idea had been to keep the Secondary School as a mixed school, and then really to fill up the educational frame work by a high school for girls., to correspond with the Graminar School for boys: It was quite ivscandal that the•chil- dren of the upper and middle classes could not get the education they needed in the town, but had to go out of Warrington. A town the size of Warrington should be able to give its bays and •girls of all classes the education they needed. (Hear, hear)
Which is the " Better Class" ?
If they made the Secondary School into a school for girls Only and the Grammar School into the secondary school for boys, he doubted

whether the boys and girls of the classes to which he had referred would attend them. It might be said it was snobbish, but Ile had no snobbish notion in his mind at all. The boys and girls would not be .satisfied to go to the secondary schools in the town. The better class, better, that was, according to the present state of social development, would not go. Mr. JOLLEY Which'is the better class?

Alderman BENNETT said that iie ;;;--s.o demo- cratic in his ideas that he believed the better class was often found in the working class, but he was speaking of the world as they found it. It was quite certain that nless some accommo- dation of that character was found in War- rington they would soon find that the boys and girls would be sent elsewhere to be educated. lie thought it ought to be possible for any boy or girl to get the education they desired in Warrington. There was distinct room for schools of different types, because of the differ- ent types of education. It seemed to him that the existing Secondary School naturally would devote itself to the more practical side of educa- tion, the scientific, technical side, and he thought,there was yet rooinfor a—school in War- rington to keep up the old tradition of classical education and specialise in literature, art, and music.
A Horrible Danger.

There was a horrible danger in the fact that they had become such a commercial country and ignored every form of education except that which turned into smoke, chimneys and earning large fortunes. Mr. R. T. FAmccomm: Dividends. Alderman BENNETT : Yes, "dividends." That expresses my meaning in one word better than I could express it in many. That is not the highest -education at all. While all these needs are provided for, I think there ought to be other schools wherein the older type of education can be taught—a high school for girls and a gram- mar school reorganised for boys, leaving the secondary school to perform its proper func- tions-land then going in for the more practical side of life and business careers.

The Committee's Audacity. I know I aril getting on debatable ground, but apart from all that I think that what caused me to rise was this: The audacity of the last sug- gestion. It does seem to me that it savours of audacity, or, if one may use a stronger word, effrontery. I think that is better. (Laughter.) The committee threaten to withdraw theiz grant altogether unless they 'practically absorb the school and run it as their own. At. the present moment, what are the actual figures before the committee? The governors have a capital asset of .250,000, and in addition an annual income of ..tl,lOO in. dividends and revenues, and the ,Corporation are only ex- PeOted to contribute' up to .R4OO. That Contri- bution fell to .t. 2.9 last year, yet the committee have the audacity to bay: "If you give us your etso,ooo—" The CHAIRMAN : It would be better and con- duce to a more harmonious discussion of this very important nuestion if you would not un- necessarily introduce words whiPili are not jus- tified.

Alderman BENNETT : I will try to moderate my language. " The CHAIRMAN: It will take us all our time to arrive at a friendly and satisfactory solution of this important question, and that will not be made easier hy anyone's introduction of terms and plirpses whia in themselves are not justi- fied. _ " Not Stated the Facts."

Alderman BENNETT : I am sorry if I have used any terms that are thought to be offensive, but I feel very strongly on the matter. I will give , the facts. . (Hear, hear.) In exchange for 013,100 and .250,000, we are making up a defi- ciency of .229 last year, and we are asking them to hand over this school, lock, stock and barrel. I don't think I am speaking too strongly. The CHAIRMAN: Well, you have not stated the facts; that is all. (Laughter.) Alderman BENNETT : Well, that is how the facts present themselves to my mind. Then there is a question of sentiment. I have never for- gotten, and never ea p forgive, one of this com- mittee's actions. They took over the People's College—a college that had become famous, and now the Peonle'S College is only" Arpley-street School." I hope the Grammar School, with its traditions, may not be similarly wiped out of existence. In the present case, in exchange for a small grant the Corporation have five repre- sentatives on the governing board and 20-free places out of 100 scholars admitted-10 from ele- mentary schools. Calmly to come and say hand us over all you have got and put yourself at our mercy and then we will make good "your de- , ficit " is very drastic, and I don't think that will ! conduce to " a harmonious solution." ! If the committee thought that in exchange or a continuation of their guarantee the representa- tion ought to be increased and the number of free scholars extended, he felt sure the governors would be willing to consider, the matter in the most friendly spirit. He was sincerely anxious that a solution should be arrived at which would produCe the best educational results and provide for the legitimate needs of all classes of the population. No one was more anxious than he was that their local system of education should be properly \ co-ordinated, and he was quite sure that by a spirit of mutual give-and- take that desirable end might be obtained. He thought a solution could be found without destroying the, old traditions and distinctive character of the school and without doing vio- lence to the spirit of fair play. • Councillor ARCHER seconded, and said be was surprised at Alderman Bennett's moderate lan- guage—(laughter)—in regard to the proposals. The members of the committee should rise up in arms against such drastic proposals.

MR. .JARMAN DEFINES THE PROPOSALS. Mr. J. JARMAN said that one thing in Alderman Bennett's appeal that struck him was that he gave as one of his principal reasons a strong plea on behalf of the poor -children for the re- tention of the Grammar School in its present form and some future development. After saying that he went on to say that the reason was that people of the middle and upper classes would decline to go to the SecoiplarY School. He spoke on behalf of the poor -children, who w?re considered unfit to associate - with those who went to the Grammar SOool. Itegarding ! clause 4, it _seemed to him that it was wider than some of the committee realised. It was , not:a question of a deficit up to ,k4OO. If the new building went forward and 200 scholars did , not turn up, it meant that the Education Authority would have to find £4OO, and ,might be asked to pay more than that. It was not a question of an average of ...Cl6O or £29, it was question of at least A:400, and that appeved to

have been overlooked. That was one of the reasons why the School Management Committee had made such suggestions. There was nothing in the minds of -any member of that committee closing down the Grammar School pr insisting that it should be municipalised, but if they were expected to make up, that was another question altogether. If the Grammar School governors were going to run the school on their own lines and pay for it themselves, they—in that committee were not going to object. If they were going to be asked to subsidise it, whatever the deficit might be, it was altogether another question.

"TO ENDOW DENOMINATIONALISM OUT OF RATES." Mr: Jolley's Warning. Mr. Toner said that if Alderman Bennett had read his minutes carefully before coming to the meeting he would not have said what he had. After long and careful deliberation, the School Management Committee had arrived at their decision, and he hoped their suggestion would be accepted. He did not want to go into details, but Alderman Bennett went into de- tails and Mr. Burgess, who said he did not want to discuss contentious matters, made highly con- tentious statements. The point really was: "Are you in favour of allowing public money to be controlled by private bodies?" and "Are you prepared to recommend to start the endow- ment of denominationalism out of the rates?" Alderman Bennett, frankly, seemed to be the champion of that. He (the speaker) did not think there was anyone in the town who would be against the suggestions when they had been explained properly. The School Management Committee had satisfied themselves, as far as anyone could on hypothetical figures, that the request was for an inadequate amount and in their opinion the financial proposals of the governors should have further consideration, He could - give them, further details, but it would be a breach of confidence to do so at that juncture. They had had certain details before them, and they should get hold of the fact that the School Management Committee were unanimous in their recommendations. Alderman Bennett had told them that the gover- nors controlled a capital of £50,000. If they did why should they bother that committee for £4OO or a larger sum? He was not going to lend his vote or voice to either of the two things he had quoted as being the true issues.

NOT IN PERPETUITY. Councillor PEMBERTON supported Alderman Bennett, and said if the matter was not so serious it had been amusing to listen to Mr. Jolley. He put up bogeys to knock them down again. They were discussing the minutes as presented. Were those minutes a full record? If they were not, then the members were not being treated fairly, and he would send them back. They had subsidised the school long ago, for they had passed a resolution agreeing to make up a deficit up to £4OO. Mr. JOLLEY : Not in perpetuity. Councillor PEMBERTON : We have agreed to do it. There is no time limit, and you cannot prove it is not doing its duty to this authority and the ratepayers of this town. It is doing everything it has contracted to do, and you should not break your contract. Mr. JOLLEY : We have not—

div.p: Left to the Grammar School. __

_ .... Councillor PEMBERTON : It is a most singular thing, the attack made on these schools. This committee will not be happy until every school is under the sole management of this com- mittee. The CHAIRMAN: Hear, hear.

_ Councillor PEMBERTON : I don't know where "hear, hear," comes in. This £50,000 was lest by different People for the Grammar School; and there is not the slightest doubt that the money so left is saying the ratepayers a large sum of money. _ _ _ _
Mr. G. WALKER: Question. Councillor PEMBERTON : If this Grammar School was not receiving this money the town would have to pay it. Mr. JARMAN : We are responsible for the defi- cit.

Councillor YEMBERTON : The Grammar School has been conducted in a businesslike and able manner and does its best. The governors of the school are entitled, I think, to be treated in a more courteous way than this resolution appears to me to treat them—in any way.

div.head: BREAKING THE CONNECTING LINK.
div.p: BREAKING THE CONNECTING LINK.

Mr. FAIRCLOUGH : There is another point to be raised upon this, I think. What will become of the continuation of the teaching from the lower classes to the upper classes? This is the link, I take it, and it seems to me that you break off that connection if you do this. It seems to me a very important point. We shall be able to continue the teaching from the lower classes to the higher.

WHY THE GRAMMAR SCHOOL MAY BE LEFT OUT. Mr. UPSON : It is very extraordinary how far we are getting away from the facts, and how little we understand the position with regard to the Gramniar School. As Alderman Bennett said just now, this school does, or ought to, fill a part of the education of the borough; it ought to occupy, perhaps, the most prominently placed crowning stone Of the whole educational edifice. But this authority was expressly, by Act of Parliament passed in 1902, made responsible for every form of education in the borough, and in taking into consideration what was already ex- isting, of course the Grammar School was one of the first institutions that came under our consideration, and, as Mr. Jolley ha S said, we have for years given this Fubject the deepest con- sideration. It has been the cause of endless meetings and conferences with the governors, with the inspectors of secondary schools, and with the BOANI of Education itself, and the very last charge that can be brought against the School Management Committee is a charge of want of courtesy to the governors of the Gram- mar School. (Hear, hear.) I think our patience has exceeded that of the patriarch. (Laughter.) This school, forming a part, as we want it to, form a part, of the educational system in War- rington, has been kept severely aloof from our whole educational scheme: We have to find, so far as we can estimate, higher education for about 250 boys in the borough, and, naturally, we are looking to this historical institution, as Alderman Bennett says, and we think that this might properly form 4 part of that higher edu- cation ,which is necessary for the borough, but which only provides education of one kind. Some years ago, when ,we were considering this question, we thought it would be a very desir- able arrangement for the Grammar School to take over the higher education of all the boys in the borough, and run two sides, a side which Alderman Bennett has dwelt upon, and' also a Commercial side. It is done in a great many grammar schools and secondary schools through- out the country, but we have been kept away from that position by the action, very largely, of the governors, and we have our own municipal secondary. school, and we are still kept away, and unless we can come to some satisfactory conclusion it will come to this: We shall have to run a secondary school for boys and a high school for girls, independent of the Grammar School, and the Grammar School will be left out of the scheme, regarded as sufficient for the borough by the Government. There are other questions involved.

div.head: Are the Poor Provided For?
div.p: Are the Poor Provided For?

I was surprised to hear Alderman Bennett say this school is one which will provide the neces- sary secondary education for the children of poor parents. I admit it ought to do—(hear, hear)—l admit by the terms of the trust it ought to provide free education—(hear, hear)— hut what do we &id? div.head: MOTOR NOTES.
div.p: MOTOR NOTES.

One sometimes hears motorists say, " Funny that Michelin have given up racing." But there is a reason for this retirement from the racing world, which every motorist will appreciate. To go back to the beginning, Michelin only went in for racing because there was something to learn from it. This was in the good old days before racing tyres were the monstrosities they are to-day. There was to learn that which would improve the quality of tyres for general purposes; and as long as racing could be useful to Michelin in that direction, just so long did Michelin continue to take, part in races. That these lessons bore fruit was demonstrated by the conspicuous success achieved year after year by Michelin over all other competitors—and not only on the race-circuits, but on the roads of the world at large, where motorists were finding out how great a difference lay—as it lies to-day —between Michelins and tyres of other makes. Eventually, however, there was nothing more to learn, from racing tests, to the advantage of tyres for general purposes. Speed had so in- creased that it became necessary to build ab- normal tyres, " faked " monstrosities which could stand a terrific strain for four or five hun- dred miles, but which could not, even under ordinary running conditions, do the greater dis- tances which the tourist demands.

Consequently Michelin retired from the race- track, well satisfied with the knowledge gained and with the emblems of victories achieved. Michelin left it to others to spend time and money in constructing racing freaks, and con- centrated upon the further improvement of tyres for use by the motoring public The re- sult is that Michelin Quality haa gained a longer lead than ever; and so confident are Michelin of the vast superiority of their tyres over all other makes that they are now providing motor- ists with the means of comparing the work done by their Micheline with .that of any other tyres t hey may fit. A - postcard addressed to the Michelin Tyre Co., Ltd., at 81, Fulham-road, London, S.W., Will bring a complimentary copy of this Record Book by return.

The American Department of Agriculture, after extensive study of the practice of certain poultry packers in feeding chickens with quan- tities of sand just before they are killed, so that the poultry may weigh more, has issued a warn- ing to housewives to scrutinise carefully the craws of any undressed chickens they buy, and to watch the craws of chickens that are being dressed by the butcher. Not content with add- ing legitimately to the weight of chickens 'through proper fattening processes, some of the poultry shippers, a day or two before the chicken is killed, feed red pepper which makes the fowl have an abnormal appetite, then the feed a mixture of fine sand and a little corn meal. The chicken eats this mixture ravenously, and as a result large quantities of sand are intro- duced into the craw and the intestines as well. This may amount, in the case of a single chicken, to only an ounce or two, but where thousands of chickens are sold the aggregate charge for sand becomes important, particularly where the birds are sold for Is. a pound. The housewife should not only ref ufie to buy fowls that contain sand in the craws, but should rebel against food of any kind in the crop.—"lndiana Farmer."

div.head: MARKET FOR STALE EGGS.
div.p: A MARKET FOR STALE EGGS.

It is well known that the Chinese are ex- tremely fond of eggs that are two years old, while those that are three or four years old are regarded as a particular delicacy. The "an- tique" eggs are much more expensive than new- laids. I once had a dish of two-year-old eggs, and am bound to admit 1 enjoyed them. They possess a flavour peculiar to themselves, but it is distinctly pleasant than otherwise. Professor Coulter, of Minneapolis, has been claiming that cold-stored eggs are much better than the so- called fresh variety, and that eggs grow better with age. It all depends upon the age, so the professor thinks, as do the Chinese. Unless they can be eaten when really new laid, when I think everyone will regard them as at their best, then they should be kept until the chemical change is completed. Perhaps some day our shops may be placarded with the legend—" Fully matured eggs," selling at sixpence each.

div.head: JUNE
div.p: JUNE
FARM AND GARDEN.
EARLY FARMING CUSTOMS.

Professor Walter J. Harte, University College, Exeter, in a paper he read before the Dairy Conference, said: The great expense of iron in the fifteenth century explains the fact that cart wheels were frequently made solid, cut from the section of a full-grown tree. Wooden ploughs and harrows with wooden pegs were used, and so the land was scratched rather than ploughed. The share of the plough must have been a very slight affair, having a wooden frame with an iron point to it. Steel was employed for the tips of the cutting edges of iron tools and was four times as dear as iron. Canvas had to be bought for mill sails and bags, and mill stones were a heavy item in a bailiff's accounts. Candles and suet were sometimes dearer than butter, and all fats were dearer than meat, for a cow might be made to yield milk and so pro- vide butter in winter, but the farmer could not give animals the means of putting on flesh— still less fat! So while meat was about a ; farthing a pound, fat cost about three-halfpence 'or tvopence. Candles averaged twopence a pound. They were therefore a rare luxury, and used on the farm only at lambing time. Rushes soaked in grease were the ordinary substitute for lighting purposes. The wick of the best candles was made of cotton which came from Sicily and Italy. Suet was used for candles and also for lubricating t.art wheels and mill mach- inery, and for dubbing leathers. Cows were, of course, kept for butter, cheese and milk, but the milking of ewes was also a common practice in mediwval times, and Walter de Henley esti- mated that ten ewes were as productive in milk as one cow. Milk was sold almost always at a penny a gallon. Cheese and butter were pro- duced on almost all estates, the latter being made all through the year, and it was often melted. It was used for sheep-dressing and cart-grease as well as for food. The manufacture of cheese commenced at Christmas and continued till Michaelmas. The averaged about three-halfpence a pound. ei probably The custom grew up of letting out the produce of the cows and ewes at annual rents, the cows at about six shillings a year and the ewes at one shilling, the "deye" taking the risk and the owner supplying the food. The reason sug- gested for this plan is that it was almost im- possible for the bailiff to check the management of dairy.

_ Eggs, poultry, and also pigeons were exceed- ingly abundant. Honey did not fetch a high price. Professor Rogers thinks that bees were not commonly kept, but it looks rather as if bee-keeping was nniVersal, and that there was,. therefore, tr.market for honey. It was certainly much used instead of sugar, and also in the manufacture of mead. The same authority thinks that rabbits were introduced into Eng- land about the year 1200., As they seldom wander more than a hundred yards fiom their homes they would spread very slowly. They were quite dear in 1270, the price being fivepence each. There were very few vegetables; onions, leeks, mustard, peas, and possibly cabbages and nettles were grown in the gardens; apples, and some- times pears, in the orchards. Ale, made with- out hops, and eider were drunk in great quan- tities. Wine also was made in England, but not as generally as some suppose, the word "vivarium" (fishpond or warren) being mis- taken in manuscripts for " vinarium" (vine- yard). MILK CERTIFICATES.

Mr. Samuel's promise not to oppose a pro- posal that milk should be certified by official autlmority according to its quality has given great satisfaction to producers. They would welcome a clause in the Milk and Dairies Bill making suitable provision for the sale of certi- fied or graded Milli. They believe that the solu- tion of the milk problem will be found in giving official countenance to classification rather than in the adoption of drastic prohibitive measures. The need for certain regulations as to sanita- tion and cleanliness is admitted, but it is held that general improvement will be expedited by statutory recognition of exceptional precaution- ary efforts in a way that will enable the pro- ducer to obtain a price commensurate with the care and outlay expended in the public interest. —"The Times." /

div.head: IN THE GARDEN.
div.p: IN THE GARDEN.

Aubrietia has become a great favourite in our gardens, thanks to the new colours which have been introduced. Some", day we may have a double variety, which would be a splendid ac- quisition. It cannot be called a rampant grower, but if it does run beyond its allotted space the plants may be cut round after flower- ing. Fowl manure is one of the richest of all fer- tilisers, containing more nitrogen than stable and cow manure. It should be stored in a dry place, and when dry be pounded into a powder. It should be used sparingly, adding three times its bulk of light soil. Used as a top dressing it is most valuable for such crops as onions, celery, leeks and other vegetables; also flowering roots. Viola Gracilas is now one of the most pleasing of rockery plants, or as an edging. It has been a mass of flowers since early in the year. Cut away suckers growing beneath the budded part of roses. These shoots are often left under the impression that they are growths of the scion, whereas They are useless.

div.head: CLIMBING. AND OWARF BEANS.
div.p: CLIMBING. AND OWARF BEANS.

Althwo—u-gh climbing and dwarf beans are already through the soil in some gardens, it does not follow that the crops will be earlier or better than those sown under warmer condi- tions. There is nothing so injurious to all plant life than a check upon its growth, and in the ease of a tender plant like the runner bean, a certain amount of risk has to be encountered if early sowings are made. The most popular dwarf bean is "Canadian Wonder." This bean was originally it climber, and by a chance a dwarf plant was discovered, and perpetuated. These dwarf beans are use- ful where sticks are not required, but most people prefer the produce of the scarlet runner. Of climbing beans there are the French and scarlet runner, the latter of which is the more hardy. If slugs abound dust around the plants with soot and lime. It is advisable to sow rather thickly, in ease of failures. They may be trans- planted to fill up gaps.

POLYANTHUS FROM COWSLIPS. " Cowslip " writes to the " Yorkshire Post " : " While on a visit last year to Bishop Monckton I had the pleasure of looking round a beautiful garden, which was mostly kept in order by an old lady. Being struck by the beautiful poly- anthus she had. I inquired where she had got them. I was taking a few roots of cowslips to transplant at home, and the old lady noticing them, told me to plant one of the roots upside down, leaves and bloom. I did so, and this year they have grown into a polyanthus,. a large yellow, a specimen of which I enclose."

CUCUMBERS IN UNHEATED PITS. Hotbeds may now be made up either in brick pits or in the frame ground, where wood frames may be used. The material should be thor- oughly prepared before the bed is made up, and this ought to be trodden tightly together before the box frame is placed in position. The soil should be allowed to become thoroughly warm before the plants are put out, and some cover- ing must be applied at night.—" The Garden."

div.head: TO ERADICATE DAISIES ON LAWNS:
div.p: TO ERADICATE DAISIES ON LAWNS:

Wrier; daisies are present to any extent they very soon crowd out the finer grasses, and means should be taken to at least check them. For this purpose there is nothing better than finely powdered sulphate of ammonia applied in dr.v weather at the rate of loz. to every square yard. This must be. repeated from time to time, and if this is persisted in, it is really surprising what an improvement can be effected in one season. The grass, of course, will take on a slightly brown tinge, but it soon recovers and comes stronger than ever.—" The Garden."

div.head: CYCLISTS' NOTEBOOK.
div.p: THE CYCLISTS' NOTEBOOK.
Who Conceived the Idea of Balancing on Two Wheels?
TO SHAKESPEARE'S COUNTRY.

A month ago I sketched an outline of this route as a return from Chepstow. I will now, in time for the holidays, give the forward journeY by the most direct road, and, as it hap- pens, the one with the best surface and least smoke. All Warrington cyclists can find the best way to Holmes Chapel (20), and from thence to Newcastle (16). The rise into Stafford- shire is amply repaid by the long, gradual descent into the Pottery town, and the coal dis- trict hardly affects this road. The fcaNvard run to Stone (9) may be varied by crossing Trentham Park., until, lately the seat of the Duke of Sutherland. I can recommend the Granville Hotel at Stone. The splendid road along the Trent Valley is at last quitted at Armitage (19). Lichfield (5), with Dr. John- son's Old house and the magnificent cathedral, is the first large town of interest. Coleshill (10) is too far out of Birmingham to be spoiled by it, but until Kenilworth (13) is reached the in- fluence of the great city can be felt and seen. Of course, the castle is the attraction of Kenil- worth and is well worth visiting. By making Warwick a stopping-place, a great many places of interest may be visited. Stratford is nine miles; Guy's Cliff lill is two, and should on no account be omitted; Leamington is two, and the old Roman Fosse Way is four miles beyond the noted Spa. Henley-in-Arden via Claverdon (10), Barford (4). Charlecote (7), where William was convicted of poaching the deer, and Ann Hatha- way's cottage at Shottery is two miles beyond, Stratford. Leaving Stratford to return, the Avon road is traversed to Eveshain il5), and Pershore (7), and the Black Country may be again dodged by coming home through Worcester (9), Stowport (12), Bewdley (3), Much Wenlock (22), and Shrewsbury (I 3 We are then 52 miles from Warrington.

div.head: MORE TINKLES.
div.p: MORE TINKLES.

We passed, last Saturday but one, on our way to the Forest, a pretty, half-timbered, thatched cottage at . Bartington Cross-roads, tenanted by Mr. Withinshaw, with a lovely gar- den round it. At nine o'clock we passed the same place. The cottage was burnt from end to end, the garden was a puddle, and all the neighbours were connecting the fire with a traction engine that we had also passed at Acton Swing Bridge. These pretty thatched cottages are disappearing fast enough, in all conscience.

Anyone who goes to Hatchmere need not be afraid of lacking accommodation for tea, for Harilman's have been putting up any amount of substantial wooden tents to house parties of nearly any size. With the miles of free forest road at hand, and the big playing fields belong- ing to the noted caterer, no one need say Hatch- mere is a dull place for an afternoon's holiday.

div.head: FROM "THE PALL MALL GAZETTE," APRIL, 1899.
div.p: FROM "THE PALL MALL GAZETTE," APRIL, 1899.

Who wa's the first man to conceive that he could keep upright on two wheels, one in front of the other? Presumably a movable front steering wheel was introduced long before pedals or cranks were attached, for my father (born 1804) has often told me how he coasted down many a long hill on his dandy-horse when he was a young man. Would not the fact of a rider feeling himself able thus to maintain his balance be likely to suggest that momentum only was necessary to keep the machine from falling?

div.head: -LAST SATURDAY'S CLUB RUNS.
div.p: -LAST SATURDAY'S CLUB RUNS.

Wesleyan C.C.—Whilst Warrington was wel- tering in waterfalls, we were wending our way to sunshine at Helsby. The Guild Sports were made more successful by the presence of 40 cyclists. Alter Sutton Weaver was passed not a drop of rain was encountered. An excellent tea was served in the Wesleyan Sunday School by the ladies of the Helsby Guild, and then the ,climb of the hill commenced. The road home ,was taken over Kingwood Hill to Kingsley, and Acton Bridge was reached at 9.15. I will describe this most fascinating route next week under "Rides with an object."

St. George's.—Settirday''s inclement weather robbed us of one Of our prettiest rides. It was our intention to make the circular route through Lyman. Birkin Heath and Ashley, re- turning through Postkerne and High Legh. As ' it was, however, tile rain caused a considerable curtailment of Our programme and Broomedge was only reached at tea time. 'After tea the weather was a little kinder to us, but it was not deemed expedient to continue much further, and accordingly an early return was made via Boothbank and High Legh. CLUB RUNS TO-DAY. Warrington C.C.—J'adgate (bowling). Warrington Wesleyan.—Davenham. Sankey Bridges Wesley Guild.—Peover. St. George's.—Delamere Forest.

div.head: CHURCH AND RELIGION IN DAY SCHOOLS. National Society Activity.
div.p: THE CHURCH AND RELIGION IN DAY SCHOOLS. National Society Activity.

Strong views were expressed against the closing down of Church schools at a meeting held in connection with the National Society at the Patten Hall, Winmarleigh-street, on Wed- nesday. The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton presided, and many of the local clergy were present in the audience. The Rev. W. J. Elsley (vicar of St. Anne's, Stanley) and the Rev. F. H. Cooke (Northern organising secretary of the society) delivered addresses upon the work and claims of the National Society. •

div.head: REV. E. C. E. CARLETON AND "PARENTS' ------- –
div.p: REV. E. C. E. CARLETON AND "PARENTS' ------- -
RIGHTS."

In his introductory remarks, the CHArizatts referred to the question of religious teaching. He could not understand why the local Educa- tion Authorities should question the honour of the schools; but, whatever happened, they would, by mearls of the National Society, defend the trust and their teachers' and the parents' rights in the question of the religion that should be taught their children. (Applause.)

ROMAN CATHOLICS AND NONCONFORMISTS. The Rev. W. J. 'ELSLEY said he was sure that if the Church only made a firm stand it would be successful. To-clay children were being turned out untrained in the fear of man and God.

_ The Roman Catholics would not allow a single school of theirs to be closed, even if the Church and the Nonconformists would; so that in a few years the position would be that the only schools giving definite religious instruction would be Roman Catholic. Most of the Noncon- formist bodies were lamenting the decrease in the number of Sunday school scholars, and at the Wesleyan Conference two years ago it was stated that the reason for this was the lack of religious teaching in the day schools. If this was not remedied they would never reach them in later life,. and a ' large section of Noncon- formist Churches were now realising that the shutting up of Church schools was injuring them. The Church was training children under a definite religious influence, as they should do, at the most impressionable period of their lives.

div.head: Education Not Instruction.
div.p: Education Not Instruction.

' They must .remember that religious education was not instruction: it *as character training. Therefore the non-theological and non-dogmati- cal Bible training advocated by Dr. Clifford must never prevail. Churchmen could never allow the Bible to be taught from a literary and his- torical point of view, because, if so, there went 'Christianity What, then, was the use of teaching at all? Fear of Denominationalism. -

...... In conclusion, Mr. Elsley emphasised the im- portance of the "teacher" question. Ile would never allow a child to be taught 'Christianity by an atheist, for a child quickly realised whether its teacher believed what he taught. Many teachers nowadays were afraid to teach very much, for fear the instruction bt:came denomi- national. (Applause.)

div.head: "STUCK TO HER GUNS."
div.p: "STUCK TO HER GUNS."
The Rev. F. H. COOKE said there never was a time when the outlook of the Church schools
(Continued in next column.)
POLITICS IN THE HOME.
Would Votes for Women Lead to Cat and Dog Life P LIVELY ADULT SCHOOL PAPER.
At the Sankey Bridges (Men's) Adult School last Sunday Mr. E. Lowe, of Penketh, gave a lecturette on "The Women's Movement."

The speaker said that those who looked deeper into this question realise that it is some- thing more than a mere struggle for a vote. It is a demand for the rights of citizenship. Mr. Lowe asked who gave man his authority to dictate to woman what laws she shall obey and what rights and privileges she shall and shall not enjoy. Man has taken this authority on himself, but he is beginning to realise that woman is becoming conscious of the fact that she ought to take her place with man in the social and political life of the country. Legis- lation in the past has been altogether one- sided, the interests of woman have never been seriously considered. Many arguments are used against woman's admission into the Councils of the State. Woman is not able to defend her country, it is said, and therefore she ought not to enjoy the same rights as a man. Does mother- hood count for nothing in the State? Are the soldier's mother and wife of no account? It is absurd to, assert that al mother and a wife has no stake in the country. She must go on send- ing her sons to the. wars, she must weep if he is sacrificed, andl his, wife Must still mother his orphans, but her opinions on the political causes of the instrument which robs her of her loved ones are of no account. That is her legal position by .man-made laws. Then there is the old worm-eaten argument that a woman's place is in the home, looking after the husband and children. True enough, if she has them. But the taking of an interest in communal and national life need not make her less lovable as a wife or a mother. Nay, rather it should in- crease those qualities. Apply the argument to I men. A man has a business which keeps him occupied all day, but no one suggests that he should be disenfranchised for fear of neglecting it; yet the moment women begin to take an active interest in public affairs we hear a great deal of fuss about neglected homes. There is nothing in the franchise for woman which would interfere with a woman's ordinary work any more than it does with that of a man.

div.head: Needless Fears.
div.p: Needless Fears.

There is also the hypothetical difficulty of the diffeeence of political opinion across the break- fast table. Domestic peace cannot be secured by suppression, but by its expression. The fact that a Liberal or Labour man marries a woman from a Tory nest does not mean a cat-and-dog i life. There are deeper things n human life which keep the kalance. The objection that woman may become too powerful a factor as a voting quantity need disturb no one. The franchise extended to woman will not bring about the alleged sex war, because of the natural law that woman and man are complimentary, not antagonistic. Then it is asked: What will the vote do for woman? The answer is: All that it has done for man. It has enabled men conscious of com- mon interests to get those interests looked after. Even to the smallest group it makes a difference between having a little power and no power at all. Again, it enables a man to complete his education. Consider again all the legislation concerning children. What right has the State to exclude the mothers from taking their full share in moulding the laws respecting their off- spring. . Once men 'realise the contribution which women could make under present condi- tions to the social and educational life of the country, the franchise will be granted. The school did not accept all Mr. Lowe's opin- ions, and an interesting discussion followed.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH MEN'S.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH MEN'S.

Considering the wet morning, there was a large attendance on Sunday to hear Mr. James Ball give a very interesting lecturette on " The Ethics of Robert Louis Stevenson." The lec- turer was keenly followed and many questions were asked and much information was given by the speaker.

div.head: LONGFORD MEN'S.
div.p: LONGFORD MEN'S.

On Sunday morning a lecturette on "The House Fly" was given by Mr. J. A. Bradley. The subject was both instructive and well dis- cussed. The Bible lesson on "The Hebrew Prophets of the 7th Century: The Heroes of the Long Dark Years," was introduced by Mr. Broadhurst.
At the close of the school an interesting pre- sentation of two chairs—one for the use of the President and the other for the Secretary—was made to the school by Mr. John Hickman, of IWest Bromwich.

div.head: LOCAL WEDDINGS.
div.p: LOCAL WEDDINGS.
NEIVALL-ROBERTS.

A pretty wedding took place at Lloyd-street Wesleyan Chapel, Llandudno, on Thursday week, when Miss Annie Roberts, only daughter of Mr. Daniel Roberts, motor coach builder, who resides at Grosvenor Villa, St. Mary's-road, Llandudno, became the wife of Mr. James Newsll, jun., eldest son of Mr. James Newsll, of " Drachanfels," Lower Walton. The bride- groom is employed at Messrs. Forshaw's Works, Warrington.

The ceremony was conducted by the Rev. Thomas rtughes, and Mr. Ernest James played the Wedding March and other suitable selec- tions upon the organ. The bride, who wore a charming dress of white satin, trimmed with pearls and ninon, carried a bouquet of carnations, lilies and white heather, and was given away by her father. The bridesmaids were the Misses Gertie Jeffries, Susie Allen and Phyllis Deacon, and the best man Mr. Harold Newall.

After a reception had been held at Grosvenor Villa, the happy couple left for Edinburgh, where the honeymoon is being spent. At Messrs. Forshaw's works on the previous Saturday morning a handsome set of twelve fish carvers was presented by the employes to Mr. Newell on the occasion of his approaching marriage.

div.head: MORRIS-WHrTFIELD.
div.p: MORRIS-WHrTFIELD.

The wedding was solemnised at Wycliffe Con- gregatiopal Church on Thursday week of Miss Catherine Whitfield, second daughter of Mr. Robert Whitfield, of 121, I3ewsey-road, and Mr. Ernest Morris, of Beech Villa, Lymm. The ceremony was conducted by the Rev. T. T. James, and Mr. W. IL Payton played suitable musical selections upon the organ, including the Wedding March. The bride, who was given away by her father, 'was becomingly attired in a dress of blue satit. broche, and carried a bouquet of pink carna- tions. Miss Mary Whitfield (sister of the bride) acted as bridesmaid, and wore a dress of flow- ered voile, carrying a bouquet of sweet peas. The duties of best man were discharged by Mr. Frank Morris. A reception was held after the ceremony, after which the bride and bridegroom left for Scotland, where the honeymoon is being spent. The bride's travelling costume was of Saxe blue, with hat to match. Many handsome presents were received from friends and the bridegroom's co-workers on the staff of Messrs. Crosfield's.

div.head: MOSS-LLOYD-JONES.
div.p: MOSS-LLOYD-JONES.

A pretty and interesting wedding was solemnised on Thursday at Latchford Baptist Church, when Miss Winnie Lloyd-Jones, eldest daughter of Mr. and Mrs. E. Lloyd-Jones. " Cartrefle," Fairfield-road, Latchford, was married to Mr. Ben Moss, son of Mr. Jos. Moss, Stockton Heath, by the minister, the Rev. J. S. Chedburn. Miss Gertrude Jones officiated at the organ. The bride, who was given away by her father, was charmingly attired in a Wedge- wood blue silk crepe dress, trimmed with bro- cade silk, and wore a Leghorn hat, trimmed ' with a large ostrich feather and pink roses, and carried a bouquet of pink roses and lilies of the valley. She was attended by two bridesmaids,— Miss Edith Jones (cousin of the bride), who wore a pale blue silk dress and black picture hat trimmed with white plumes, and Miss Phyllis Lloyd-Jones (sister of the bride), who was attired in a white embroidered voile dress and Leghorn hat trimmed with blue ribbon and forget-me-nots. The best man was Mr. Jos. Moss, jun. (brother of the bridegroom). The reception was held at Atkinson's Cafe, after which the happy couple left for Llandudno, where the honeymoon will be spent. The bride travelled in a navy blue costume and Tuscan hat. Many handsome presents were received.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 27, 1914. PASSING WEEK.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 27, 1914. PASSING WEEK.
THE FIGHT FOR TIIE GRAMAIAR SCHOOL.

The real question at issue between the Educa- tion Committee and the Governors of the Grammar School was brought nearer the surface on Monday night than has hitherto been the case. Councillor Pemberton, who has a facility for blurting out truths which other persons avoid, called the discussion in the Education Committee an " attack " upon the Grammar School, rand added: "This Com- mittee will not be happy until 'every school is under the sole management of this Committee." To this Councillor Henry Roberts made the brief but significant remark, "Hear, hear." Mr. A. J. Jolley, as a Churchman and Conservative, was exceedingly frank when he said that the points the Committee had to settle were: Were they owing public nioney to be controlled in favourtrollektbyp of llbodies? and Were they pre- pared to recommend to start the endowment of denominationalism out of the rates? Councillor Roberts, in winding up the • discussion, intimated that he would be 'pleased if an amicable settlement could be arrived at, but , the lines set forth by the recommendations submitted were the "main lines upon which the Committee intends to proceed."

" TIIE AUDACIOUS ULTIMATUM." Those lines, which are set forth fully in our report, briefly are that the Committee cannot be responsible for an indefinite period for any deficit up to .R4OO a year in the accounts of the school; and that further 'financial assistance from the rates will only be considered "on the basis of the municipalisation of the Grammar School." The Education Committee desire that the school, if a new one is to be built, shall be dovetailed into our public educational sys- tem, if we are publicly to contribute ta its up- keep. The Governors wish to maintain the school as at present, and, as Mr. Jolley puts it, the public are asked to "endow denomination- alism." A great, deal , was said about the £50,000 assets of the Governors and the income they derive from the benefactions Of the past. Alderman Bennett spoke warmly about the "deliver or die ultimatuni " that had been pre- sented in return for assistance from the rates, which, last year, amounted to only £29; hut these points were met by Mr. Upson, who said that -the benefactions were not left to the pre- sent Governors, but for the education of "the children of Warrington," and by Mr. Jarman, who said that the responsibilities of the pro- posed new 'and enlarged schoor would be greater than those prevailing in the case of the Present school. Nlr. Sawkins Burgess; who champions the cause of the Governors, .ex- pres,sed the hope that he two authorities might settle the question in a quiet and amicable manner. The Chairman' agreed, but he added.: "Always bearing in mind this fact, .that this authority is the only body upon whom., the responsibility for making adequate provision for education of all kinds in the borough finally rests, and in any grant of the public money there must be such control as would justify the Committee in making the grant." The Com- mittee decided, by a very large majority, to send their "audacious" ultimatum to the Board of Education, who had asked whether the Com- mittee would be prepared to continue the guarantee if the Governors built the new Grammar School.

RADIUM AND CANCER. s, It seems strange that, at a time when Nature has yielded up one of her secrets and shown how one of the most dreadful ,and dreaded of diseases may be fought with sonic hope of suc- cess, appeals for funds to apply the knOwledge we have should be made in vain. Manches- ter—rich and prosperous Manchester—Opened a fund months ago in order to raise £25,000 with which to purchase radium, but £B,OOO only had been raised by the beginning of this week, and a special meeting was called to discuss ways and means. Dr. Dawson Turner, who came specially from Edinburgh, to make a special appeal, pointed, out that a dozen years ago all the wealth of the world could not have obtained for a sufferer the heal- ing virtue of this rare substance. You who are well-to-do can afford to command this treatment if in need of it, but the poor, who are always with us, and who always will be, in spite of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, cannot obtain this Privilege except by your charity tbrouo the hospitals. Will you, who possess the means, not liberally help to mitigate the ravages of cancer amongst the poor by strengthening the hands of those who are qualified to administer this life-prolonging stance? and pain-subduing sub- Warrington, we doubt not, will. be asked to assist Manchester, and thus become entitled to share in the benefits of the possession of a supply of radium, which is far too eNpensive to be bought in sufficient quantities by the smaller communities. •

THE COUNCIL AND IIE ALTII.' There is a good, healthy Understanding among Englishmen that they shall not judge their fellows unheard ; but the few members of the Council who met at the Town Hall to (ifs,. CUSS the report of the Medical Officer of Health on NtiTednesday night, and had to abandon the plan because, they were not sufficiently runner- ous to form a legal meeting, did not wait. Alderman Bennett suggested that the absent ones should be s.ealped by their constituents when election 'time comes round; but .there may have been extenuating circumstances' if not, actually good excuses in most cases. A nice, balmy summer evening is a great temp,ta- Lion in a climate where they are so very scarce.

div.head: WHAT DOES HE MEAN?
div.p: WHAT DOES HE MEAN?

.. We notice, not without a feeling akin to anxiety, that Mr. HAROLD SMITH, M.P., has been telling the Women Tariff Reformers that he intends to lead a most aggressive attack upon the Liberal party; neither giving .nor ask- ing any quarter: It is not-the flrSt time he has said the same thing recently. We wonder what he means, and why he persists in talking in the language of the battlefield. Perhaps it is "a bit of Ulster," as a member of the Education Committee called a threat on. Monday night. We should also like to know about when Mr. SMITH thinks he will start upon his merciless cam- paign. We learn from Brewer's Dictionary of Phrase and Fable that to grant quarter is "to spare the life of an enemy in your power." Our lives are . scarcely at the disposal of Mr. SMITH, as yet, which is perhaps fortunate since he is in such an unbending frame of mind when the battle is so far away. Dr. Tusler says of the phrase to grant quarter, "it originated from an agree- ment anciently made between the Dutch and the Spaniards that the ran- som of a soldier should be the quarter of his pay." "probably," is the cOm- ment of Dr. Brewer, "it simply means to grant conditions ; hence its mean- ings of kindness, friendship and good- will—allied to cceur " [heart]. So that Mr. SMITH, even if the sedondary mean- ing be given to the words he uses,. is going to,grant us no conditions, nor is he going to show us any kindness, friendship, or goodwill. Worse than that, he expects us to give him no quarter, but shut him off from all kind- ness, friendship, and goodwill. 1 It will be remembered that less than ,a year ago LADY GREENALL herself spoke pf the preference •she had for hatred where Radicals Were concerned. This was at a Women's Tariff Reform gath- ring, and at the annual meeting of hat great organisation the note of hate AA,'-as again sounded in cold blood and Oold print. We can but hope that these mutterings are onlv meant in a Piclswickian sense ; but it seems I:t ,trarige that this gospel of hate should 'always be preached when Women Tariff Reformers are about. So far as we know the mind of the Liberal party, its members are desirous that the com- ing contest shall be, fought without bitterness, and witha dignity becoming the great causes of freedom, equality, and progress that we shall champion. Tilft,;, causes stand on their own merits :111d do not need bolstering up by pre- judice or rancour. If our opponents think they stand in need of opposite methods we shall regret it:; and, as liampions of retaliation, they must not :omplain if they, get their own wings i-tair.ed a little. Mr. SMITH, to do him ustice, says he will not ask for quarter. lit we will ask him, and those with 'horn he associates to study, with •actical ends in view, those lines •hieh, a a lawyer and an amateur !tor, he will know very well :

Sale at Lymm. Messrs. A. II Clive and Co. will sell several desirable dwelling-houses and cottages at the Plough Hotel, Lymm, on Wednesday next, to commence at six o'clock. The solicitor is Mr: T. Ridgway, 2, Cairo-street, Warrington.

div.head: PROTECTION AND CON-SCRIPTION.
div.p: PROTECTION AND CON-SCRIPTION.
Mr. Crosfield Says a Bad Way to Support A Bad Purpose.

div.head: Music in the Park.
div.p: Music in the Park.

_ The R.A.0.8. Military Band will play selec- tions in Bank 'Park to-morrow afternoon, under the conductorship of Mr. Robert Smith; and on Wednesday evening Messrs. Peter Walker and Son's Band will occupy the stand.

div.head: Seinions.
div.p: Seinions.

Sunday school anniversary services will be held at the Emmanuel Reformed Episcopal Church, Bold-street, to-morrow at 10.30 a.m., 3 p.m., and 6.30 p.m. The, offertories will go to the Sunday School Fund.

div.head: Bachelor of Laws.
div.p: Bachelor of Laws.

_ Mr. Richard H. Albery, M.Sc., principal of Earlestown Technical School, late second master of Warrington Secondary School, has obtained the Degree of Bachelor of Laws of the Univer- sity of Liverpool, and has been awarded first- class honours.

div.head: BSc. for Warrington Student.
div.p: BSc. for Warrington Student.

Miss Gladys Joynson, daughter of Mr. Frederick Joynson, Museum-street, and a former student of the Warrington Secondary School, has obtained the degree of Bachelor of Science of the University of Liverpool. She is the second daughter of Mr. Joynson to take a degree. - \ .

• Bo Wlllllj Prizes. The silver challenge trophy and prizes given in cennection with thet Warrington Works' Bowling Association Competition are on view in Mr. Craik's outfitting window in Butter- market-street.—The beautiful prizes, other than the trophy, hake been supplied by Mr. F. Hal- lett, jeweller, Bridge-street, Warrington.

Warrington Dealer and Magistrate. A Warrington scrap iron dealer and pawn- broker, Charles Humphries, 13nttermarket- street, Warrington, waS committed to the Staf- ford Assizes on Thursday from Brierley Hill Cot on a charge of uttering a defamatory libel concerning Mr. W. W. Doughty, chairman of the Tipton justices, and a County Councillor.

Oppressed Baptist Missionary. , A resolution was passed unanimously at Gol- borne-street Baptist Church on Sunday night relative to the imprisonment of the Rev. J. S. Bowskill and his native helpers at San Salvador. Copies of the resolution were forwarded to the Foreign Secretary, Sir Edward Grey, and the local Member of Parliament.

div.head: Disastrous Ride.
div.p: A Disastrous Ride.

Whilst riding on the drawbar of the trailer of a heavy motor car, Fred Read Barrow, a youth, of Hall-lane, Sankey, fell off, and the trailer passed over him. First aid was rendered by Arthur Fisher, employed at Messrs. Cros- field's works,-and at the Infirmary it was found that Barrow was suffering from a crushed foot and other injuries.

Temperance Work. There was a good attendance at a meeting under the auspices of the Warrington Band of Hope Union, held on Monday night on land near the Ellesmere-street Mission. Mr. J. W. Bradley occupied the chair, and an address was delivered by Mr. T. D. Leslie. Songs and reci- tations were given by the Misses Ada Hamer, i Annie Edwards, Annie Williams and May Elliot. Miss Eva Tanner (the Temperance Queen) was present and persuaded a number of people to sign the pledge.

Staff Trip. A pleasant outing was enjoyed by about 28 members of the staff of Messrs. Rylands Bros., Ltd., who left for Llangollen in the forenoon of Saturday last in the well-appointed motor char- a-banc of Messrs. Middleton and Wood, of Wigan. After a beautiful drive through Weaver- ham and Delamere, Chester was reached at 12.30. Following lunch in the city, the party pro- ceeded; via Wrexham and Ruabon, to Llangol- len. The party, after having enjoyed some of the best views that North Wales can provide, returned, and reached home about half-past ten.

Emmanuel Church Choir Trip. The choir members and friends of Emmanuel Church, Bold-street, held their annual outing on Saturday, Liverpool and Niew Brighton being the places visited. In the morning the liners Victorian, of the Allan line, and the Adriatic, of the White Star line, were boarded, and many interesting features were seen. After dinner the time was spent in visiting the various places of interest at New Brighton, and the party went to the Vale Park Gardens for tea. Warrington was reached•at ten o'clock, a very enjoyable day having been spent.

Warring ton Woman's Suicide at Bolton. A terrible discovery was macle in a dwelling- house in Bolton early on Monday morning, when Sarah Burke, wife• of Michael Burke, licensee , of, the Mersey • Hotel, Warrington, - was found lying dead with her throat cut. An inquest was held the following day by the Bolton Coroner, when the husband said the deceased had been suffering from nervous depression.- She had been., under the . care of a Warrington •doctor, who advised a change of air, and .at her request she was taken to ,Bolton a fortnight ago. • Kate ,Greenhouse, wife of Daniel Greenhouse; said the woman had been stiWing, with her, and had been very much depressed. She had several times expressed the wiskth at she was dead, and said that if she was not such a coward She would make an end of herself. She retired to bed with witness on Sunday night, and was then a}Tar- entlY in good spirits. In the morning witness missed her, and on going downstairs found her lying on her back behind the back kitchen door, with her head in a pool of blood. Her throat was cut, and there was a razor lying on a table close by covered with Mood. • A verdict 'of "Suicide whilst temporarily insane" was returned.

div.head: Presbyterian Carden _Fete.
div.p: Presbyterian Carden _Fete.

In connection with St. John's Church, and in continuation of the financial effort, of which the recent successful bazaar was the chief ex- pression, a most enjoyable garden fete was held on Saturday in the grounds of " Newholme," Latchford, the residence of Mr. W. Russell. an active member of St. John's Kirk Session. The garden and lawns were looking their best; gaily decorated as they were for the occasion with a profusion of flags and bunting, kindly supplied and fixed by the courtesy of Mr. R, Hutton, of Messrs. Peter Walker and Son. Tea tables were • arranged on the lower lawn,' where tea was served to about 200 people. Excellent selections of music were played by the Latchford Orches- tral Society, under the conductorship of Mr. A. Grounds, and contributed very materially to the afternoon's enjoyment, as did also the efforts of the St. John's Pierrot Troupe, composed of Misses G. Clark, Wrench and Mounfield, and Messrs. A. G. Lewsey, R. Mungall and J. Aitken, all of whom preyed themselves 'capable enter- tainers. Clock golf and bowls found numerous patrons amongst both ladies and gentlemen, whilst all were reminded of the business aspect of the function by a work stall and refreshment stall arranged on one side of the larger lawn, under the charge respectively of Mesdames Leiper, Walker and Robertson, and Mesdames Leigh, Bowen and Murray, with assistants. The ladies showed they had lost none of their bazaar energy and persuasiveness, and the result will be a considerable addition to the church build- ing and special funds.—ln the evening dancing was indulged in on the lawn to the music of the orchestral society, and kept up till dusk, when the party broke up, all feeling much indebted to Mr. and Mrs. W. Russell for so kindly having placed their grounds at the disposal of the mem- bers and friends of St. John's.
