div.head: 'EXAMINER, SATURDAY,
div.p: THE 'EXAMINER, SATURDAY,
Change of County Court Judge. Judge Stanger, K.C., our County Court Judge, has been appointed to the Bristol Circuit. He will be succeeded by Judge Henry Edward Gurner, of the North-Eastern Circuit.

div.head: Colonel Warburton's Will.
div.p: Colonel Warburton's Will.

- A sum of £60,042 was left by the late Colonel Piers Egerton-Warburton, 8.A., of Arley Hall, Northwich, formerly honorary colonel of the Cheshire Yeomanry, and Conservative M.P. for Mid-Cheshire from 1876-1885.

A Young Cuckoo. A pair of titmice are bringing to a fine state of maturity a young cuckoo which has been hatched in their nest to the exclusion of their own young, which they built in a tuft of grass on a neglected grave in the Cemetery. It is expected that the young monster, which is three times the size of the nest on which it lies, will fly to-day.

The Church Society. A most encouraging report • was read by the Rev. G. Vale Owen at the annual general meet- ing of the Warrington Church Society, which was held iii the Church House, Bridge-street, on Monday evening, when the Reetor (th 9 Rev. Canon Willis) occupied the chair. Mr. 'C. A. Littler (hon. treasurer) submitted a satisfactory, financial statement, which showed balance in hand of .e 27 12s. Bd. The officers were re-elected.

div.head: Scottish Weddinti.
div.p: The Scottish Weddinti.

What was probably the last chapter in the curious " Scottish Wedding" tangle was heard at the Warrington Borough Police Court yes- terday, when Mr. A Browne applied on behalf of Sarah Platt, 69, Knutsford-road, for an order respecting one of the children. Mr. T. S. Steel appeared for William Speed, tramway man, 35, Wash-lane.—An order was made for ss. and a guinea costs.

Early Morning Fire in Sankey-street. The shop occupied by Miss J. Cox, tobacco- nist, 24a, Sankey-streetwas discovered, about one o'clock on Thursday morning to be on fire. Mr. Connor's chauffeurs, who made the discovery, attacked the fire with buckets and summoned the brigade, which arrived under Superinten- dent Turner and prevented the outbreak from spreading. The Chief Constable and a number of his men rendered valuable assistanc.

div.head: Professor Armitage.
div.p: Professor Armitage.

At the annual meeting of the rorkshire Inde- pendent (Congregational) College, Bradford, held on Wednesday, reference was made to the loss sustained by the retirement of Professor E: Armitage, whom the governors have now elected Professor Emeritus of the College. The Professor, whO has preached many times' at Wycliffe Congregational Church, and is conse- quently well known in Warrington circles, has now completed 30 years' service at the College, and a handsome portrait in oils was unveiled there to mark the event.

div.head: Cliffe Sermons.
div.p: Cliffe Sermons.

The Rev. A. E. Robinson, of Manchester, con- ducted the annual summer sermons at Hill Cliffe Baptist Church on Sunday. The choir gave anthems at both morning and evening services. Madame Sara Silcock and Miss Emily Tayllor rendered the solos very creditably. The special morning service for young people was presided over by Mr. S. Brocklehurst, and Mr. W. H. Wallington gave the address. Miss Bate, of Latchford, gave the solos. Tea was pro- vided for visitors in the schoolroom, and the day's collections (for the church funds) totalled £26 6s. 6d.

div.head: Presbyterian Anniversary.
div.p: Presbyterian Anniversary.

The anniversary services of St. John's Sab- bath School of the Presbyterian Church are being held all day to-morrow, the special preacher being the Rev. J. G. Tosh, minister of Rochdale, and moderator of the Manchester Presbytery. The music, to which the scholars will largely contribute, will be in keeping with the occasion. The entire offerings at the after- noon and evening services are to be devoted to the school funds. The Sabbath school anniver- sary this year, as previously, culminates in the picnic to Frodsham on Walking Day. The arrangements and prices will be as usual.

div.head: Iron Broker Sued.
div.p: Iron Broker Sued.

At the Warrington County Court on Thurs.- day, before his Honour Judge Stanger, James Prescott, Bridge End Bone Works, Church, sued Charles Starkey, iron and metal broker, Mersey-street, Warrington, for ..t45 10s., damage's for breach of contract on the sale of a benzine plant. Mr. Heys (lOssrs. 'Reddish and Heys), of Accrington, appeared for the plaihtiff, and Mr. R. K. Chappell, Liverpool (instructed bY Mr. T. S. Steel, of Warrington) for the defend- ant.—After Mr. Heys had stated the case for the plaintiff, the parties consulted, and Mr. Chappell intimated that they had agreed to judgment for the plaintiff for £13.105.. and taxed costs on Scale "A."—Judgment was entered accordingly.

A Workman's Claim. The hearing was resumed at the Warrington County Court on Thursday of the case in which John Henry Appleton, Synge-street, Warring- ton, applied for per week from the end of October up to the present time, from the Pear- \ son and Knowles Coal and Iron Co., Ltd., in respect of an • injured eye, which he received whilst working for the respondents at 31illom, in Cumberland. From October to the 14th of January he earned £1 12g. 10d., which was £1 less-than his average wages, and -since January he had not worked, being, it Was-alleged, totally incapacitated.—His Honour said that after con- sulting with Dr. Bowden (the medical assessor) he had come to the conclusion that there must be an award for the applicant, but the amount was a difficult question before him.. The im- pairment of vision would prevent applicant doing work as a rivetter. The effects of the accident had not disappeared and there was an impairment of vision, which was by no means trifling. He Made an award for 15s. per week from January 10th, with costs. Mayor and Mayoress Busy. The Mayor and Mayoress have had a full programme of civic duties this week. On Mon- day they were guests at a garden party in Liverpool, and on Tuesday his Worship, with Alderman John Evans and Mr. Gray (water engineer) rkeived a large number of members of the Royal Antideluvian Order of Buffaloes from Southport who had motored to Warring- ,a no ug r Provincialcimes ,G Grand ltolnaSterTißlerapdabrutyr;. other local members, motored to Houghton Green Waterworks,Coittee hadwhere the- WaterethneewCheanigrminaenstoafited for the first time. At the invitation of the mm tli Mayor the party partook of refreshments. Qn, arrival at Warrington the visitors were taken round the Park and greatly admired the con- servatories. Dinner was served ,at the Lion Hotel, and the party afterwards visited the HipAdrome and finished at the "Duke of Lan- caster" Lodge he4dquarters.—A hearty vo-ke of thanks was accorded the Mayor and Alderman John Evans.—The 'Mayoress was amongst the guests at the St. Helens Mayoral garden party given on Thursday by Sir David and Lady Gamble at Windlehurst. •

(- Catl,et Battalion C.L.R. The annual inspection of the 2nd Liverpool (No. 11) Cadet Battalion, on behalf of the General Officer, Western Command, Chester (General Sir H. McKinnon), took place (by kind permission of the Principal of the Warrington Training College) in St. Elphin's Park on Thursday evening. The Inspecting Officer was Captain F. Nicholls, Northumberland Fusiliers, Adjutant 9th Battalion King's (Liverpool) Regi- ment. The battalion, with its colour, was drawn up in line under the command of Major Brooks, and the Inspecting Officer, who was accompanied by the Assistant Chaplain (the Rev. W. Bracecamp) and Lieutenant-Colonel Appleton, C.L.8., commanding the battalion. made a minute inspection of the whole batta- lion. The battalion was Then put through a few movements by the Commanding Officer. The Inspecting Officer after- wards said that two things particularly im- pressed him—the great steadiness in the ranks while he was inspecting them, and the cleanli- ness of the carbines. He complimented the band upon its smart appearance and upon its playing, and said that the company drill and the extended order were both good, and he was struck with the quickness of Movement. He also expressed approval of the work of the signallers and ambulance sections. Out Of a total strength of 150, there were 138 of all ranks present on parade.

11 assisting at the recognition of work in the Cause of humanity such as Alderman Burton had been engaged upon for many long years. (Applause.) Alderman Burton was formerly . deputy-chair- man of the committee under the late Alderman John Roberts, and since he took over his pies- • ent position, eight years ago, he had encour- aged the working men to further efforts. In 1880 they had only .t 165 as the year's contribu- tion from the committee to the Infirmary; now they were raising about £1,300 a year; and, giving credit where it was due, he thought they must give Alderman Burton the bulk of it. (Ap- plause.) Their Chairman was one of the prime movers in the scheme for collecting in the works, which had proved so successful. (Hear, hear.) He (the Mayor) had felt that he would like to show the members of those two committee's and their wives some slight recognition of the noble work in which they were engaged—he did not think it had been their lot Tin to the present to have a civic garden party. They deserved every encouragement to proceed in their good work on behalf of the Nursing Association and the In- firmary. When they read letters like the one he saw that morning in "The Examiner,'' signed by parents. of a child inmate, congratu- lating the Infirmary upon the care and success- ful treatment of young childreo, he thought they spoke volumes, and should do much in reaching the hearts and opening the pockets of all who were in a position to assist the funds of the Infirmary. (Applause.)

The Mayoress, who carried a bouquet of pink carnations, presented before the proceedings opened by Miss Lulu Hampson, daughter of the Hon. Secretary of the Working Men's Infirmary Committee, was charmingly attired in a gown of embroidered lawn, trimmed with Brussels lace. She was accompanied by the Misses Wil- kinson, Mr. and Mrs. Timmins (the Mayoress's father and mother), and Ar. and Mrs. Brockle- hurst (the Mayoress's sister and brother-in- law). Among those also present were : Alderman Thomas Burton (chairman Work- ing Men's Infirmary Committee), Mrs. Pearson and Miss Burton; Mr. J. George Walker (chairman District Nursing Association Working Men's Committee and vice-chairman of the Infirmary Committee), T. C. useful work in the town. The older committee,tbe Working Men's Infirmary Committee, was estab- lished in 1880, and had, since that date, con- tributed no less than 0224,000 to the funds of the Infirmary. (Applarfse.) The committee of the Nursing Association, which had been in exist- ence only eight years, had made a contribution of about .21,600 to the funds of their Association. (Applause.) He thought nll would agree that the two committees bad shown a real live inter- est in these two very important institutions. Their necessity was regretted, but still they were indispensable, and they must be sup- ported; and he was glad to say that, notwith- standing the circumstances that had arisen dur- ing the last eighteen months, the working men of Warrington had risen to the occasion and had effectively and worthily contributed to the main- tenance of thee institutions. One factor in their success was that the working men's corn, mittees consisted of a large number of repre- sentative men from the several works of the town; and he thought the Mayor would recog- nise in the men before him that they were at least a very fair sample, and did credit to those ! who had elected them. (Hear, hear.) The presence of the ladies, too, would no doubt serve a useful purpose, because they hoped to enlist ,! the sympathy of the working men's wives in ! the noble work the committees bad in hand, for, having that sympathy, they would command .eyen greater success than in the past. They hail all classes of opinion on the committees—

not have been present had not a taxi cab come to his door, the driver having had instructions to bring someone here. (Laughter.) He knew nothing about this. lie had been associated with the Working Ven's Committee for many years, and witnessed the advance of their con- tribution from £lOO and something to between .C 1,300 and £1,400, and during the whole of that time and work he did not know that anything had been kept back from him; ,he had taken a deep interest in the Infirmary even before the committee was formed; and when Buckley-street Church was organised he had a great deal to do with the drawing up of the deeds, which pro- vided that the property should revert to the Infirmary if ever it ceased to fulfil the purpose for which it was erected. In all his long experi- ence he had never been kept in the background when anything was going on.

"Until to-day," declared Aldermap. Burton, " the committee have always been loyal to me. I have been kept posted up; but to-day someone has gone behind my back, and this is the pickle , they have placed me in. (Laughter.) I don't know what to do, but you know, ladies and gen- tlemen, this [Mr. George Walker] is the horse that always carries any saddle that we put upon him, and I should not be surprised if he is ro- sponsible. (Mr. Walker: "No, no.") And the Mayor. (The Mayor: "No" and "No guesOng." and laughter.) I shall leave it for him to make any explanation; and I shall never forget his 1 kindness as long as I live." (Cheers.)

Alderman Burton's Golden Wedding. Surprise. • The reception was enlivened by a presentation made to Alderman Burton, chairman of the Working Men's Infirmary Committee, on the occasion of his recent celebration of his golden wedding. It was a surprise gift, the worthy
kept in till the last
ignorance moment. assembled on the si Chamber, and whi'
clock the company :eps leading to the Council the Mayor ostensibly ex-

politcal,, social and religious—yet they had managed to steer clear of all those complications that might • . cause discord. That the Infirmary Committee largely owed to the fact that they - had to preside , over them Alderman Burton. -- (applause) I —whose tact, goodwill and geniality had no doubt smoothed over some of those corners that i'.were apt to present themselves on occasion. l'Alderman Burton had had the loyal support of every member of the committee in anything he had originated for the benefit of the two insti- • tutions. Alderman ;Burton, as he deserved to have, had had a very successful matrimonial life and had recently celebrated his golden wed- ding. (Applanse.) It was celebrated very privately, but that did not prevent some of his friends congratulating him. 'We. of the Working Men's Infirmary Com- mittee," concluded Mr. Walker, were very anxious to add our congratulations, and to ex- press the hope that Alderman Burton may he spared to rule over our deliberations for many long years to Come, and that there may be many bright years in the future for both him and Mrs. Burton. (Applause.) The committee thought they would avail themselves of the -opportunity afforded by the kindness of the Mayor and Mayoress to present Mr. Burton with this solid silver fruit stand, with our very best wishes for is and his wife's future welfare." (Loud aP- lause.)

The hiayor's First Job. The Mayor, whose kindness (along with the Mayoress) that day they would always remem- ber, was the first president of the Working Men's Infirmary Committee; they would agree that he was a jolly good president, too. (Ap- plause.) He mos'ed a hearty vote of thanks to his Worship and Mrs. Peacock for the kind and generous way in which they had entertained the committees. Mr. T. WADSWORTIL seconded, saying they had extended a privilege that had never before been bestowed upon the committees.. The vote was carried by acclamation, and calls foil cheers for the Mayor and Mayoress were responded to with much heartiness. The MAYOR, replying, said he had only done his duty, and he would be pleased to do any:. thing he could in the future to encourage them in the work in which they were -engaged. They had evidently wanted some ornamentation, so they made him their first president. He had absolutely nothing to do—
Mr. GEORGE WALKER :Id this is his first job. (Laughter.) .
The MAYOR: lila if you get other Mayor to take on the same jet) I shall be satisfied.. (Ap- plause.)

What Distinguished Washington. Richard Croker, at an open-air luncheon at Palm Beach, told a George Washington story. "A teacher," he began, "Was conducting a lesson in history. "'Tommy Jones,' she said, 'what was there about George Washington which diStinguished him from all other Americans?' "'He didn't lie,' was the prompt answer."

Councillors Who Fail to Discharge
Their Duties.

To consider the Medical Officer's annual report, a special meeting of the Town Council was called for Wednesday evening, bilit had to be abandoned owing to there being 13.4. quorum. Twelve members constitute a meting, but there were only the following terx: members present ten minutes after the time fixed to begin:—
The Mayor (Councillor Peter Peacock). The Deputy Mayor (Councillor Dr. Joseph).
Alderman W. Pierpoint. Alderman A. Bennett. Alderman James Evans. Councillor J. Pemberton. Councillor J. Shaw. Councillor R. Henshall.
Councillor Dr. Fox.
Counciflor S. Gough.
The Deputy Town Clerk (Mr. Holloway) and the Medical Officer of Health (Dr. G. W. N. Joseph)yere among the officials present. _ . . _

The MAYOR, after having waited about twenty minutes, said he was pleased to see some mem- bers of the Council had turned up, but he re- gretted that they had not a quorum and was sorry that they could not hold the meeting. Alderman JAMES Evaxs (chairman of the Health Conlmittee): Have you no power to ad- journ this meeting? The .Alixoa : I cannot adjourn a meeting that is not alive. Alderman BENNETT expressed indignation at the dereliction of duty on the part of members of the Council in not attending. Alderman Eva/is: I should think it is of suffi- cient importance. I move that the names of those who have attended be recorded. The MAYOR: I have discussed it with the Deputy Town Clerk and he has ruled that we cannot adjourn the meeting.

Dr. Fox: Could not Alderman Evans give us an outline of what he was going to do?, Alderman EvAxs : I do not know. If the mat- ter is going to be broached at the next 'Council meeting the points will certainly be raised.

A VERY IMPORTANT MATTER. Dr. JOSEPH: There are some very interesting points in the report. It is like a captain taking the position of a ship. We want to know where we are in this very important matter. I feel not only indignant, ,birt very regretful that we are in this very -humiliating position. I do not know whether it is a 'vote of censure on the Health Committee, but it locWs very much like contempt. The MAvoa; Of course, it is very unfortunate that the Chairman of the Health Committee and the Medical Officer of Health will be away for the next meeting. Alderman EVANS : To do all this, furnishing a report, making preparations to speak on its important points, and then to meet in Council— I look upon it as ignoring us. Councillor PEMBERTON : The only possible way would be to arrange a meeting to be held after the next meeting of the Council.
The MAYon: but the Council is not here to make arrangements. Councillor PEMBERTON : I think with the Deputy Mayor that it is of sufficient import- ance.
Councillor riENSHALL : Would it not be practi- cable to call the meeting for 5.45 before the Council meeting?
The MAYOR: It could be if the requisition was signed in the legal way.

WHAT WILL PEOPLE THINK? Alderman EVANS : Does it not look like con- tempt; and what will it look like in the eyes of the public or other municipalities if we have to drag on, for consideration of our Council, our report until the time when we are getting • material together to compile another report? Alderman BENNETT : hope that when the ratepayers read the report of these proceedings they will note how many so-called representa- tives are failing to do their duty. I do not think it is the Health Committee. I think they are to blame who take upon themselves duties which they fail to discharge. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Gomm: Are all the members of the Health Committee here to-night? The MAYOR: No, they are not. (Laughter.) The members then retired.

ROYAL COURT THEATRE.

div.head: "The Great Detective."
div.p: "The Great Detective."

We are shown how a daring and desperate gang of criminals are tracked down by an ama- teur, but very clever, detective, his assistant and a bloodhound, at the Royal Court Theatre, this week, and the change from orthodox melo- drama is quite refreshing. Needless to say, there are many exciting, sensational and humorous incidents, and these are made the most of by Carlotta do Yonson's Company. Mr. C. Douglas Carlile gives a very impressive por- trayal of the ready-witted, cool and active detec- tive, and Mr. Lee Gilbert ably assists him, anl also indulges in many highly diverting pranks. As the "Old 'ILI," Mr. C. A. Carlile is capital in the role of leader of the gang, and Mr. Charles Clifford plays the part of the swell crook" in thoroughgoing fashion. Miss Ca.-- lc.tta De Yonson makes a successful appeal as the emotional Sal Williams, whilst Miss Minna Green as Claire Vernon acts the part of the " dupe" with equal skill. The other parts Are well sustained by Messrs. Roy G. Stoll, Arthur Miller, Chris. Harding, Alex, Waters,. C. H. Tracey, Teddy Hay, and Miss Maria Janson.

The excellent programme, attracting large houses this week at the Hippodrome, includes Billy Spears, who has cleverly trained his dog "Lady" to perform numerous tricks. The Two Geor,tsis conclude their splendid hand-balancing act by one jumping over five standing men and being caught by the hands and held in mid-air by the other. The Record Quartette's spectacu- lar banjo act supplies many novel features, in- cluding an amusing banjo sermon by the "Rev. Baystring," and they are loudly applauded for their, ragtime selections. Happy Attwood creates considerable laughter by his parodies on popular songs; whilst Kendrick and Laura supply thgtime music and dance in a clever / fashion. The High Davos Company perform their acro- batic roller-skating Af-ith ease and grace, and the Perfection Pictures are "The Iron master and "Furnishing Extraordinary "—drama an humour respectively. div.head: BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
div.p: BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
MONDAY.
_ Before the Mayor (in the chair), Alderman W. Bolton, Councillors G. W. Joseph and J. Wil- kinson, Messrs. S. Wright, W. Roberts, G.

Pilling: and W. Furness. Through the Window.—Timothy Parsonage. labourer, 26, Jockey-street, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Winwick-road on Saturday.—The evidence showed that he fell through a window, but prisoner attributed this to slipping on a piece of banana skin.—He was fined 45., including costs, or seven days. Irishmen in Trouble.—William Fahay and Martin Fahay, farm labourers, of no settled abode, were charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in Market-street on Saturday. The first prisoner was also charged with assaulting a man named Thomas Kenny, who, it was stated, gave him no provocation whatever.—William was fined 10s. and costs and Martin ss. and costs. Deserted.—William Ashall, private in H Corn- party, Depot, South Lancashire Regiment, Orford Barracks, was charged with being a deserter since June 206.—Acting-Sergeant Ed- wards said he was called to a lodging-house in Barbauld-street on Sunday, when, in conse- quence of information he received, and seeing the prisoner wearing a military shirt, he arrested him.—The Chief Constable said they understood prisoner had sold sinne of his mili- tary clothing, which was proof, of desertion.— Prisoner was handed over to a military escort. Licences.—Albert Widd, of the Pied Bull Hotel, Newton-le-Willows, was granted tempo- rary authority to sell at the Roan ,Cow Hotel, Latchford, in place of the present licensee, Mrs. Margaret Hackney, who is retiring. -Mr. H. J. Longton made the application. William Broughton, of 78, West-street, was granted tem- porary authority to sell at the Lord Rodney, in Winwick-street.
TUESDAY. Before Councillor H. Roberts (in the chair) and

Mr. C. Jackson Holmes. Another Chance.—John Bennett, 6. Enfield- street, was again charged with neglecting his 4 children.—Mr. A. Browne prosecuted.—The evi- dence showed that since the prisoner was before the Court preciously he had been fairly good from time to time, but eventually he resorted to his old habit and would not go to work. A gentleman had taken an interest in the family, and by a subscription a bedstead and bedding had been provided.— Prisoner's wife said she did not wish to have her husband dealt with, for he had been upset.—The Chairman said it was a most difficult case; it was ad- journed for a month, but if, in the meantime, there was any cause for prisoner to be brought before the Court the case would be heard.

Destructive Boys.—Aaron Longworth, 14, Gas- kell-street; George Wilkinson, 34. Laira-street; and liarry Monaghan, 56, Sharp-street. all boys, were summoned by Christian Bower. 430, Knuts- for.d-road, for destroying growing rhubarb, and doing damage to the extent of is—P.C. Titylor said he was on duty in Bridge-street on June 13, when prosecutor came to him, saying he had the defendants detained. When at the Police Sta- tion the defendants admitted the offence.—Mr. Bower said he could not say what amount of damage was done, as it was a daily occurrence. —The cases were dismissed on payment of costs. From the Pawnshop.—Mary Prescott, 64, Dal- ton Bank, was charged with stealing a pair of men's boots from the shop of Mr. Thomas Dom- ville, pawnbroker, 69, Church-street.—The evi- dence showed that prisoner was in the shop the previous day pledging a ring. She was wearing a shawl and placed the boots underneath as she was leaving. Later she made an attempt to Pern them at Jackson's shop, which was not far away from the place from where they were taken. Owing to the police having circulated a description of them, prisoner was apprehended. —The case was dismissed on payment of costs, the Chairman remarking that prisoner would feel her position keenly.

div.head: THURSDAY.
div.p: THURSDAY.

Before Messrs. J. Rymer Young (in the chair). W. Roberts, A. J. Jolley, and Dr. Naden. Trick Cyclists.—Percy Haigh, 43, Fox-street;l Samuel Knight, Rose Villa, Hallsfield-road ; and James Gleave, 21, Powys-street, were charged with furiously riding bicycles in Kendrick- street on May 29th. They were fined 10s. each, the Chief Constable stating that he had to compliment the boys on their cleverness, as they were loaded with newspapers. It was marvellous how they were not thrown off their cycles.—Sergeant Kenwright proved the case. Sunday Gamblers.—Albert Abbot, spreader, 25, Lloyd-street; Harold Spooner, labourer, 40, Lloyd-street; John Davies, labourer, 30, Lloyd- street; William Leah, labourer, 7, Lloyd-street; John Millington, clerk, 44, Mill-lane; Joseph Eccles, apprentice, 62, Selby-street; Joseph Woodward, labourer, 19, Powys-street; Alfred Lawton, labourer, 119, Cartwright-street; James Hargreaves, labourer, 69, Priestley-street; John Kinsey, labourer, 39, Leicester-street; and Wil- liam Colsy, labourer, 160, Evelyn-street, were charged with gaming at the rear of Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co.'s Works with cards on Sunday, June 7th. Kinsey and Woodward did not appear.—The evidence showed that the police detected the defendants playing in two gangs and saw money pass between them. They ran away when they observed the police, but two who were caught gave the names and ad- dresses of the remainder.—The Chairman, in fining the two absent defendants 12s. 6d. each and the remainder 10s. each, said the offence was had enough on a week-day, but was still worse on a Sunday.

div.head: CHILDREN'S COURT. WEDNESDAY. Before Messrs. S. Wright _(io ,the chair), • J.
div.p: CHILDREN'S COURT. WEDNESDAY. Before Messrs. S. Wright _(io ,the chair), • J.

'Upson, and A. J. Jolley. " Money for Walking Day."—A twelve-year- old girl was charged with stealing a pair of boots from the shop, 69, Church-street, in the occupatien of Mr. Thomas Domville, pawn- broker.—The Chief Constable said the girl was sent to the pawnshop, and shortly after she had left the shop the boots were missed. Tho matter having been reported to the police, the girl admitted that she had stolen the boots to get money for Walking Day. The Education Auth- ority had nothing against the girl, who, how- ever, frequently ran, away from home, and had been guilty of pilfering.—The girl was dis- charged with caution. Window Breaking.—Eleven boys were pro- ceeded against for wilfully breaking windows in the works of Messrs. Bowman, chemical manufac- turers, Lythgoes-lane.7-Mr. Mottrami-of Messrs. R. Davies and Co., who prosecuted, said' that he did not think any firni suffered more from the wilful and wanton destructive element. There was also a danger to the boys themselves if any of the carboys containing vitriol exploded, Forty-One windows were broken and the total damage amounted to,, £2 4s. 6d.—P.C. Hussey Proved the case.—Each defendant was cautioned ' and fined ss.

Boy Carnblers.—Seven boys were charged with gaming on the approach to the Central Station Goods Yard.—P.C. Dixon proved the case.—Five of the boys were licensed newspaper sellers and promised to give up their badges. When ques- tioned, one of the boys said he was doing it "to win money," and another boy caused amuse- ment when, in reply to the Chief Constable, lie said they did not all win.—The boys were cau- tioned and fined is. each. Stone-throwing.—For throwing stones at a telegraph pole, two boys, 15 and 16 years of age respectively, were each fined 10s., including costs.

Railway Trespassing.—For trespassing on the London and North-Western Railway and expos- ing themselves to danger, four boys were each ordered to pay 3s. mother stated that she could not see how the boys could move wag- gons.—The Chief Constable: I did when I was their size and lam sure they can. (Laughter.)

div.head: e. !STRICT fIEW3
div.p: e. !STRICT fIEW3
STOCKTON HEATH
TOWNSHIP TITTLE-TATTLE.

At last! Our local Councillors have a chance Of making light of a dark subject. The Ship Canal Company do not object To the Council lighting the Swing Bridge. By electric light. Certainly not. It will be a cheap guide to mariners. . For the present, however, The matter has been deferred, So there is no fear of the Bridge people Seeing a ship any sooner and Thus delaying many "Heathens" longer than at present. We are progressing! Fancy, we can claim to have what Warrington has— A smoke nuisance. One Councillor says it is a frequent occurrence For chimneys to be fired on Sunday mornings, And a parish sweep is suggested. One "Heathen" jocularly remarked That the reason why this nuisance Has not been noticed before is that Councillors do not wear white waistcoats Or winter Sunday morn:ags Another official needed in the village Seems to be a parish baker To provide loaves, Which one Councillor suggests sl.uuld be placed On the trees, to prevent the horse: E the bark whilst waitingi for their T driversaotifi vent girls. ungish their tete-a-tete with the pretty ser- Of course, the "Heathen" who stated That it did not go properly dark On Sunday, which was the longest day. Had the advantage of his listeners, Who gave the lie to the assertion That birds—night birds—of a feather Flock together. At least we can get a quorum At the Council meetings— Which was more than Warrington could do On Wednesday, when there should have been A special meeting to discuss The Medical Officer's report.

Parish Council.—At the meeting of the Stock- ton Heath Parish Council, held on Tuesday evening, there were present: Councillors Mc- Intyre (in the chair), Hallows, Whitley, McDer- mid, Westbrook, andolie Clerk (Mr. E. Brad- shaw). -

Parochial Committea—The members present at the Stockton Heath Parochial Committee meeting on Tuesday were Councillors G. Pilling (in the chair), W. Mantyre, J. Hallows, J. Whitley, J. McDermid, H. J. Westbrook, and Messrs. T. H. Warburton (deputy clerk) and S. Wright (surveyor).

Boy Wanderer.—Found on a Stockton Heath road on Tuesday morning, a boy, aged four- teen, named Patrick Cody, was handed over to the Rochdale police and charged at that court on Wednesday, under a warrant with having failed to observe the conditions of recognisance entered into by him under the Probation Act.— The Chief Constable said that the previous morning the boy was found on a road at Stock- ton Heath, near Warrington. He had a mania for wandering.—The boy expressed a desire to be a sailor, and he was sent to a nautical school at Liverpool until he is eighteen years of age.

Recreation Ground.—The question of a recrea- tion ground for Stockton Heath was again men- tioned at a meeting of ;the Parish Council on Tuesday, when the Clerk (Mr. E. Bradshaw) said that some time ago a small committee was appointed to consider the question, and at one of their meetings they decided to communicate with the Arley estate agent and the Wilderspool. Brewery Company respecting the land. He had written to the Arley estate agent four or five times, but had only received a reply to his first letter. A reply had been made by the Brewery Company.—After Some discussion the Chairman (Mr. W. Mclntyre) agreed to interview the Arley estate agent.

Corporation's Offer to Supply Electricity.— At the meeting of the Stockton Heath Parochial Committee on Tuesday a letter was read from the Warrington Corporation giving a formal in- timation of the Corporation's intention to apply to the Board of Trade for a Provisional Order authorising them to supply electricity to Stock. ton Heath and other parishes. The application was to be made immediately. The -communica- tion stated that the Parochial Committee were in favour of the proposal.—Councillor West- brook said this was not so. They did not sup- port it, neither were they opposed to it.—Coun- cillor Mclntyre agreed.—Councillor Westbrook: We did not assume an active attitude; our part is a passive one. (Hear, hear.)

Houses and Land.—A number of figures were read at the Stockton Heath Parish Council on Tuesday relating to information sought by the Council as to the cost of building workmen's houses at Leigh.—Councillor Westbrook: How can anybody on this basis say land stops build- ing? In this case the land required costs .020, whereas the rest of the expenses comes to .1:21,270. The Clerk (Mr. E. Bradshaw) : Or, in other words, twenty times as much as the price of the land.—Councillor Westbrook: It is ridiculous.— Councillor Whitley said over 20 houses were being built.—Councillor Hallows: And there are several empty now.—Councillor Westbrook: The cost of labour is responsible for the big te There a there r price for the building of those houses at Leigh. hTtlti naoreutnbirontshe tooftohrecre up the cost of land,

The Smoke Nuisance!—" There is rpom for another Government official—a parish sweep. Cannot sckmething be communicated to Mr. Lloyd George?" said Councillor Westbrook at the meeting of the Stockton Heath Parochial Committee on Tuesday evening. The statement wound up a short discussion arising out of a report of the Sanitary Committee, when it was stated proceedings were to be taken against a person for allowing a chimney to be on fire.— Councillor Hallows said it was a frequent occurrence, especially on Sunday mornings, and sometimes when people were going to places of worship. Heath-street was noted very much for this. (A Member: It is.) It *as very bad last Sunday in two places.—Mr. E. Bradshaw: Sweeps do not want to work on Sundays. (Laughter.)—lt was upon this that Mr. West- brook added the statement already quoted.

div.head: PARISH " CHOP." Horses AA Melt Eat Bark Off Trees.
div.p: PARISH " CHOP." Horses AA Melt Eat Bark Off Trees.

At the meeting of the Stockton Heath Parish Council on Tuesday evening, in the 'Council Schools; Councillor Whitley said he had re- ceived complaints respecting the hawkers' horses, which, while the driver was calling at houses, were eating the bark off the trees. The horses were sometimes five or ten minutes with nobody in charge. _ _ _
Councillor Westbrook : The police can deal with that.
• _ The Chairman (Councillor Mclntyre): It is only supposition that the damage is caused in this way:_ _

Councillor Westbrook: I hare seen it. The Chairman: Oh, well, the attention of the police ought to be called to it-. Councillor Whitley: I saw one to-day, and the Ilriver confessed to it. Councillor Westbrook : Why not put a nosebag on? Councillor McDermid : It is a matter, for the police. Councillor Westbrook: It is rather hard lines for the man in charge. The Chairman: stated that a recommendation should be made that the horses should be better fed or that the owner of the tree should hang out a loaf of bread or supply "chop." (Laugh- ter.) . . _
Councillor Westbrook: There is Another thing —to find parish "chop" for horses. (More laughter.) It was ultimately decided that the attention of the police should be drawn to the matter.

div.head: LioniNG OF THE SWING
div.p: THE LioniNG OF THE SWING
BRIDGE.

The question cf the lighting of the Stockton Heath Swing Bridge was again mertioned on Tuesday evening at a meeting of the Parochial Committee. Councillor Whitley read the following letter from the Manchester 'Ship Canal Company's General Superintendent (Mr. Latimer), dated from the Dock Office, Manchester, on May 29th: "Dear Sir,—tiorthwich-road Swing Bridge. Referring to your letter of the 6th inst. forward- ing copy of a resolution which was passed by the Stockton Heath Parochial Committee..... The Canal Company will have no oblation to grYit the permission asked for, provided the plAcing and maintaining of the electric light is subject to and satisfactory from time to time to, the approval of the Canal Company's Chief Engineer." Councillor Whitley, continuing. said they had held a meeting of the Lighting Committee that night, when the matter was considered and the following resolution passed : "That the matter , respecting the lighting of the Ship Canal Bridge by electricity be deferred until we can ascer- tain whether we can obtain a sufficient power of electricity for the proper lighting of the bridge, and also to make inquiries respecting the charges.".... He moved that that be passed.
Councillor Mclntyre seconded. This was agreed to. Councillor McDermid : Will they see the ships sooner than at the present time? Councillor Westbrook. They see them soon enough now. (Laughter.)

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

Old Scholars' Re-union.—The annual re-union of old scholars took place on Saturday at the Friends' School, Penketh. The parents and scholars arrived about 11 o'clock. accompanied by the Secretary (Mr. J. Spence Hotivson). Dur- ing the afternoon cricket matches between for- mer and present scholars were played, the Old Boys winning by three runs, and the Present Girls beating their predecessors by 90 to 20. About 100 visitors partook of tea, and during the evening various games were indulged in and greatly enjoyed by all. The fine weather added to the pleasant remembrance of a most enjoy- able afternoon.

• Labour Meeting.—On Wednesday evening the Labour party held a meeting on the Recreation Ground, Penketh, when Mr. Seddon gave an address, and was emphatic on the need of more sympathy and consideration between masters and men. The meeting was well attended, the other speakers being Mr. Lewis and Mr. Thorpe, Mr. Gill occupying the chair.

div.head: ORFORD.
div.p: ORFORD.

Coronation Excursion.—Difficulties having stood in the way of the erection of an ornamen- tal lamp with the surplus money raised for the Coronation festivities, it was decided to use it for a half-day excursion for all the school chil- dren residing in Orford, and children now liv- ing outside the village whose parents contri- buted towards the Coronation funds. About 170 children, accompanied by some parents and friends, accordingly spent an enjoyable day at Southport last Saturday.

div.head: WIN WICK.
div.p: WIN WICK.

Cricket.—Winwick Asylum entertained Leigh Wesley Guild on. Saturday and were defeated by one wicket. Only three batsmen reached double figures for the home team, G. Dawson (45, in- cluding seven 4's), J. Walsh (21, with six scoring strokes, five 4's and a single), and W. R. Walker (16). For the visitors N. Gilman took seven wickets for 36 runs. For the home team C. Cunningham took five wickets for 44 runs and I'. Hilton three for 30.

Successful Druids' Main.—The members of the "King. George V." Lodge of the Order of Druids held a successful bowling main at the Hermit Inn. After many keen games the semi-finalists were Messrs. J. Farmer and W. Yates, and C. A. Peckett and J. Jones. The game between Far- mer and Yates was very keen at the commence- ment, but, getting his opponent on a favourite mark, Farmer ran out an easy winner by 13-7. Peekett and Jones had a .stiff struggle, Jones failing to score with four yards to win in at the last end, Peckett winning by a single. In the final Farmer won by one.

Friendly Society Gathering.—On the occasion Of the initiation of Mr. R. Forshaw, County Councillor, as an honorary member of the King George V." Lodge of the Order of Druids, there were rejoicing at the IThrmit Inn, Winwick, on Saturday, when Bro. W. Wood: D.D.G.M., presided. He stated that during recent years the social side of the lodge work was fast flisappearing, and was being re- placed by a business spirit which was very much regretted, as it Was through members meeting together in a friendly and social spirit that Friendly. Societies owed their present proud position. ,k Applause.) He was glad to see that the members of that Lodge were keeping the old friendly spirit going.—Bro. Beckett assured Bro. Forshaw that the members of the Lodge were very proud to have him as one of their four honorary meinbers.—Bro. Forshaw, in reply, strongly urged the members to foster the spirit of self-help, and when they took up any- thing, no matter what it was, to excel.—The following were the artistes at the smoking con- cert: Messrs. E. Smethurst, Roberts, Richards, Forrest, Garnett and R.. A. Chandler. Mr. Q. H. G. Bon was the pianist.

div.head: CROFT.
div.p: CROFT.

Unitarian Chapel Anniversary.—The annual c!I a pel and school sermons were preached at the ( roft Unitarian Chapel on Sunday, when the Rev. It. Stuart Redfern, of Swinton, was the special Preacher. At the afternoon service the anthem "lify His Name" (G: E. Martin) was r reit, and at the evening service Martin's" lest, breathe an evening blessing." was sung- The music at both services was sup- plied by the Warrington Unitarian Choir. The collections amounted to about £l4.

div.head: JUNE 27, 1914.
div.p: LYMM.
Church Army Meetings.—Capt. A. Pickersgill and Cadet A. Stephens, of the Church Army, are conducting a series of meetings in the parish, which so far have been well attended.

Pastor's Progress.—The Rev. J. A. Penaliggon, pastor of the Congregational Church, is making fairly good progress towards recovery from his illness. -He is at present away for a lengthy. holiday, but hopes to resume his work towards the end of next month.

Sleeping Out.—At an Occasional Court, held at the Lymiu Police Station on Wednesday, William Hoyles, a Warrington loafer, and Thomas Burns, of no fixed abode, were charged with sleeping out. Boyles was sentenced to seven days' hard labour, and Burns was dis- missed with a caution.—Mr. A. Watkin was the magistrate.

Primitive Methodist Garden Party.—A very successful garden party was held in connection with the Primitive Methodist Church on, Wednesday afternoon, in the grounds of Foxley House, kindly lent by Mr. Henry Champ. There were many attractions of varied charac- ter, including races. cocoanut shies, doll com- petitions, mock art gallery, &c. A novel feature 'Was a "cobweb," which consisted of-a huge cob- web, from which issued many strings, at the end of each string all article was hid in unexpected places,- more or less difficult to find. The claim- ing of the article by finding gave rise to much merriment.—The musical part of the programme consisted of selections by the Dunham Massey Brass Band, song e by Mr. J. H. Brazendale, and violin solos by Mr. Andrews. The accompanist was Mr. Fred Champ. The Misses Armstrong and Mr. A. Appleton gave Caw performances of a little play entitled "Mischief." Several gramophone selections were given by the cour- tesy of :Miss Mabel Champ.. The whole pro- gramme was performed in a most creditable manlier, and the services of the artistes were gratuitously given, including those of the band, who were indebted to the Lymm Band for the loan of music-stands, &c.—Mr. Eric Edwards gave a very instructive demonstration of wire- less telegraphy, which was followed with great interest. Another attraction, which was very well patronised, was tho tent of Zenana (Mrs. Green), a lady palmist of surprising knowledge. ; Amongst prominent workers were the follow- , ing : Rev. R. W. and Mrs. Ferguson, Mr. and Mrs. Champ, Mr. and Mrs. Welford, Mr. and ; Mrs. Edwards, Mr. and Mrs. Cross, Mr. and Mrs. Knowles, Mrs. Colt and Mrs. Priestlier; ; the Misses M Champ, G. Priestner. B. Gregory, C. and M. Nuttall, Broome, E. Welford,'G. Wel- ' ford, H. Smith, Alice Priestlier and D. Priest- ner ; Messrs. F. and A. Champ, B. and E. Ed- wards, J. and N. Clark, A. Southall, H. Preston, Brookes. E. Taylor, S. Mairs, A. Struthers, D. Redhead and G. Redhead.

div.head: ALTRINCHAM DIVISION LIBEII %LS.
div.p: ALTRINCHAM DIVISION LIBEII %LS.
A Welsh Churchman
CHOSEN AS CANDIDATE.

The Liberals of the Altrincham Division are preparing for their effort to wrest the seat once again from the possession of the re-actionary party. On Wednesday night keen enthusiasm was manifest, when Mr. Edward Powell, of Plas-y- Bryn, Newtown, Montgomery-shire, was unani- mously selected as the prospective I iheral can- didate. The meeting of the association was 'held in the British ,Schools, Altrincham, and amongst those present were Messrs. J. H. Whit- worth (chairman of executive), F. Milne (hon. secretary), Sir A. A. Haworth, Messrs. E. H. Langdon, G. A. Pickard, Gray Pickard, William Hughes, Reginald Barker, Albert Nicholson, W. IT. Hughes, A. L. Shepherd, R. J. Matthews, S. A. Gilbody, R. P. Gregory, W. Hazlehurst, J. D. Broadhurst, W. Bowers, J. Smithson, D. M. Humphreys, J. W. Tonge, Ernest Jones, F. C. Brock, William Hill, W. R. Speechley, William , Smith, J. Smithson, E. Corrigan, William Reid, W. E. Thompson, E. M. Thorp, M. S. Newton, H. C. Clanahan, E. M. Powell, E. S. Powell, R. McDougall, J. A. Bland, J. B. Russell, F. H. Holgate, R. Owens, W. L. Feernisides, W. Pater- son, William Owen, W. J. E. Owen, Alfred
THE PROSPECTIVE CANDIDATE.
By the courtesy of the "Manchester Evening News."
MR. EDWARD POWELL„ of Plas-y-Bryn, Newtown, Montgomeryshire.
Haworth, Rev. D. Agate, Messrs. C. Hildage, W. de M. Landor, W. Fishwick, J. Percy, T. B. Parkes, and H. Hetherington, secretary and agent.

Following Mr. Powell' spirited address, Mr. Whitworth moved that Mr. Powell be invited to contest the division at the next election. Mr. E. 31. Thorpe seconded; Sir Arthur Haworth and Mr. E. Thompson supported, and it was earned. The invitation was accepted.

div.head: CANDIDATE'S CAREER.
div.p: THE CANDIDATE'S CAREER.

Born at Welshpool in 1850 Mr. Powell was educated at a private school and was articled to a solicitor in Welshpool in 1867. At the final examination he took the much-coveted Clement's Inn Prize and was admitted in 1872, and from that year until 1875 was conveyancing clerk to Messrs. Brocklehurst, Wright and Mair, of Macclesfield. From 1875 to 1907 he practised as a, solicitor in Newtown, and retirell in the latter year. He joined the Board of Humber, Limited; in 1898, and a few months later became the chairman. He was made managing director in 1905, and resigned the position in 1908. Two years later, at the unanimous requet of the Board, he re-joined, and soon after became the chairman and managing director, a .position which he still holds: No better indication of his business abilities could be afforded than by the fact that during his connection with the firm its business has greatly increased, until now about 3,000 men are employed. Mr. Powell, who is a thorough Churchman, was election agent to the late Lord Bendel, and this, together with his other campaign experi- ence, stamps him as being a "fit and proper Persou " to contest the seat in the Liberal interest.

His wife is the eldest daughter of Sir Pryce Pryce-Tones; and Colonel E. Fryce-Jones, the Unionist Member of the Montgomery Boroughs, is his \brother-in-law. Almost every Sunday he reads the lessons in the 'parish church he attends.

Mr. Powell unsuccessfully contested the Oswestry, Division at the two General Elections in 1910. He is a prominent member of the Mont- gomeryshire County Council, chairman cf tha Montgomeryshire Insurance Committee, and vice-president of the Welsla National Memorial Association. He takes a great interest in phil- anthropic movements, and recently presented the site on which(the Montgomery Infirmary is built.

div.head: WELCOME HOME.
div.p: WELCOME HOME.
Itejoieings Mark the Rector's Return
With Mrs. 114urston.

Lymm people were highly enthusiastic in their Welcome to the pretty village of the Rector and his bride on Thursday evening. The quaint streets were lined by villagers all eager to ex- tend the hand of friendship. Leaving Warrington by motor car, the Rec- tor and Mrs. Thurston arrived ar the Statham Schools shortly before seven, but their progress had twice been impeded by the old custom of roping. The first stop was on the boundary of the village, when Mr. and Mrs. Jackson, of New- field, were responsible, and the second occasion was about a hundred yards from the Stathatoi Schools, when the rope was in the hands of the Misses E. and F. Dalton and Richardson, Dr. , Thorpe, Capt. A. Pickersgill and Cadet A. ! Stephens, of the Church Army. So persistent were these people that rile Rector and his wife I found it necessary to walk to the schools, Mrs. Thurston remarking it was rather a curious thing to be arrested by a rope. A party of cheering children greeted the couple as they entered the schoolyard, and Mrs. Thurston received a beautiful bouquet from Edith Hinton, the youngest scholar, whilst two chairs were formally handed over by Mrs. Wat- son, on behalf of the day and Sunday schools and members of the Mission and the teachers. After a brief stay, the newly-married couple proceeded to the Rectory, and were heartily cheered en route. At the ancient Cross the Lymm Subscription Band commenced to play, and the bang of a rocket proclaimed the ap- proach of the couple to the Rectory. Shortly afterwards the bells in the church tower rang out, endorsing the welcome. A triumphal arch had been erected bearing on one side "Wel- come" and on the other " Health and happi- ness."

Children and their teachers collected in the gardens, and, following the presentation of an- other bouquet by Gracie Rixon, a silver salver was handed to the Rector by Marion Wright, the oldest scholar. The inscription read, "Pre- sented to the Rev. G. B. Thurston on the occa- sion of his marriage. From the teacTiers and scholars of the Lymm Day and Sunday Schools, June 9, 1914.

The Rector, speaking to the children, said: "We thank you very much for the beautiful tray, which, as you know, will always stand on our sideboard as -a reminder to us of the occa- sion." With regard to Mrs. Thurston, he was sure she would soon be as fond of them all as he had been for many years. In the evening children's sports were held in Lymm Hall Park, and the band played for pub- lic dancing. To-morrow the Band of the sth (Earl of Chester's) Battalion, Cheshire Regi- ment, by kind permission of Lieut-Colonel J. E. G. Groves, T,.D., will attend church and play selections in the afternoon. The arrangements for the reception had been well organised by the teachers and others, including Mr. F. Evans, the Rector's warden.

div.head: WARBURTON.
div.p: WARBURTON.

Parish Church Extension.—The Bishop of Chester (Dr. Jayne) attended at Warburton Parish Church on Friday of last week for the consecration of an extension to the graveyard. The clergy present were the Rev. Geoffrex Egerton-Warburton (rector of Warburton), the Revs. J. Edwardes-Evans (vicar of Ringway), A. F. White (vicar of St. Helen's Church, Rixton), and E. Edwards (private chaplain to Colonel Legh, of High Legh, and the Bishop's chaplain). The service was fully choral, the choir being under the direction of Mr. Brandon. The land ' for the extension was given by the late Lord of the Manor of Warburton (the late Colonel Piers Egerton-Warburton, of Arley). The procession to the ground, which is about a quarter of an 'acre in extent, was headed by Messrs. P. J. Leather and R. Hulme (churchwardens), and the Bishop's chaplain, who carried the staff of office. After the service, tea was provided on the Rectory lawn, through the kindness of the Rev. G. and Mrs. Egerton-Warburton.

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

Wesley Guild.—At the devotional meeting, held on Monday evening, the Rev. E. Morgan pre- sided. A short paper was read by Mr. J. Dakin on " The baptism and temptation of Christ." The roll was called by Mr. 11. Tomlin, and the lesson was read by Miss Richardson.

To-day's Walking Day.—Arrangements for to- day's Walking Day are .now complete. The procession, which will be marshalled by Mr. G. Mather and led by the Cottage Homes' Band, will leave the Railway Bridge at two o'clock in the following order :-Padgate Wesleyan School, Christ Church Sunday school, Cottage Homes children, Risley Methodist Sunday School. After passing down Padgate-lane to the end of Orford- road a return will be made to the village, and after turning at the Farmers' Arms the children will partake of tea in their respective schools.

of the a he "Sir 1 unanimousmpor n Important vote Friendly t he Gil- bert Greenall " Lodge of Loyal Oddfellows, at a meeting on Saturday held in the Plough Inn, members°l Houghton Green, decided to affiliate with the Druids as far as the/ State section of the National, Insurance Act was concerned.—Bro. George Mather, who has held the presidency of the Lodge for almost half a century, presided, and welcomed the delegates of the Order of Druids, amongst whom were the Grand Master (Edwin Allen), the Grand Secretary .(W. J. Shaw), Mr. J. Bibby (member of the Board of Management), and Messrs. W. Bibby and R. Perdue (of the Warrington district).—The small society has been in existence for over a century, but owing to the introduction of the 'sTational Insurance Scheme it was found imperative to amalgamate to other societies.—Bro. Shaw, in addressing the members, reviewed the financial position in which they found themselves, showed the terms which they. would receive if they would amalgamate with the Druids, and gave them a cordial invitation to throw in their lot with such a large and.well-established Order. —At the conclusion a vote of thanks was given the deputation, and the Grand Master, in reply- ing, welcomed the Houghton Green Lodge in the brotherhood of the Druids.

div.head: NEW VICAR
div.p: THE NEW VICAR
Inducted by Archdeacon Spooner.

The Rey. H. F. S. Collier was inducted to the living of Christ Church, Padgate, on Thursday evening. There was a large congregation, and at the commencement of the service the Lord Bishop of Liverpool dedicated a handsome oak Communion table and a brass memorial tablet to the memory of the late• Vicar, on which is inscribed: "To the Glory of God and in memory of the Rev. G. W. Dickinson, M.A., vicar of this parish 1908-1914." The tablet, together with the Communion table, was erected by parishion- ers and friends. The lesson was read by the patron of the living, the Rev. Canon Willis. A practical and beautifully-worded address was delivered by the Bishop, upon the words "There came a man sent from God, whose name was John (John i. 6). The preacher said that they met together with mingled feelings of sorrow and joy. They were sad because of their vivid memory of him who had lately laboured in their midst, but glad to receive his successor. In times of de- pression he must be patient, and must always be full of love. In these days a minister who acted as a tyrant and despot was culpable, and he was sure their new vicar would not introduce aorelties without consulting the wardens or the Church Council.

The impr-e-s-Six; Service of institution was then proceeded with by the Bishop, the induction ceremony being conduct etd at the church door by the Archdeacon, of Warrington (the Rev. Canon Spooner). A large number of clergy were present amongst the congregation. Mr. P. Blackwell presided at the organ, and the offertory was taken on behalf of the Diocesan Ordination Candidates' Exhibition Fund.

CHILDREN'S CORNER—continued.
about their native woods, painted and daubed in a savage state. However, when our ancestors did take to the

pin—that is to say when they began to clothe themselves—they took to it in earnest, and ap- peared to have been great patrons of the pin- maker. There are numerous passages up and down our old literature which seem to prove this. - Later on we come upon a very sad thing con- nected with the pin, no less, indeed, than an attempt on the part of the foreign pin-maker to dump his wares in this island. But seemingly there was a vigilant and well-organised Protec- , tionist party even in the days 4 Richard Crook. back, and an Act of Parliament was passed, somewhere about the time of the Battle of Bos- worth, stopping the abandoned foreigner from sending his pins over here. It seems • probable, however, that in these early days the pin, in this country at least, was a mere headless skewer. It is not till the year 1453, about four years before the death of Bluff King Hal, that the headed pin was introduced into this country by some French refugees. It is just about this time that we first hear Of cannon being cast in England, so that, so far as this country is concerned, it would seem as though pins and cannon are about of. an age. In those good old times our members of Par- liament looked after us properly. There was no taunt of "grandmotherly 14gislation" in those days. In 1543 an Act was passed "to avoid the slight and false making of pins." By this mea- sure it is enacted that "only such are to be sold as are double-headed, and have the heads fast soldered to the shank of the pin." The pin generally is to be " well-smithed, and shank well-shaven, and point well and round filed, canted, and sharpened." - NEM

Men thought, continued Mr. Larkin, that there was a bishop in Rome who might say a thing was white one day, black another, and neither the day after, and that they all had to follow suit. Many people actually pitied them for it. But Catholics were allowed to think for themselves—in the broad, general sense; their ! intelligence was the gift of God. div.head: "DOES GOD CARE?"
div.p: "DOES GOD CARE?"
The Rev. H. Ogden and the Lesson of the Empress of Ireland Wreck.

The Rev. H. Ogden, preaching at the Golborne-street Baptist Church, upon "The Master of Ocean and Wave," took as his text Mark iv. 38, "Master, carest thou not that we perish?" The circumstance that gave, rise to these words, said the preacher, was a storm on Lake Gennesaret. Thompson, in his "Land and the Book." mentions the suddenness of the storms that arise upon the lake. Some 600 feet below the level of the sea, and surrounded by mountains, any one of the Wadies act as a fun- nel for the wind. We complain about the vagaries of our English climate, and it is daily a matter of deep concern; but with its vagaries, generally the weather gives some indication of a change. But around Lake Gennesaret the sky may be absolutely cloudless and every indica- tion of a peaceful day given, Ina a storm of wind will rush down one of the Wadies without the slightest warning, and the surface or the lake, hitherto placid as a pool, becomes a rag- ing, tumultuous, cruel and angry inland sea. Very probably those were the circumstances which led to the storm narrated in this inci- dent. The Master was asleep in the hindmost part of the vessel, the water was gradually sink- ing the boat, and the disciples awoke Him and exclaimed " Carest thou not that we perish?" div.p: with a milk and rose complexion. Gold is much used on the millinery of the moment, and with pink may be described as the favourite colours. There can be no question that the lacquered effect on the new ribbons has come to stay. Glue is now applied to wings to give them the same appearance of extreme brilliance, and it has one advantage, it keeps thee feathers from parting in the wind, and makes them more dur- able. The sash gets lower and lower. It is still an important feature of modes. Sometimes it is simulated, or replaced by rows of narrow corded ribbon, sewn on the hips, in the position occupied by the sash. These rows serve a double purpose, since they keep down the fulness of the skirt. •

div.head: Vogue for Ostrich Feathers.
div.p: The Vogue for Ostrich Feathers.

Flowers, ribbons and feathers have all been exploited this season by rival milliners, but the victory has been won by ostrich feathers, which in the best qualities are more seen than ever. They are used in novel ways. Very lengthy ones form the sole trimming of black velvet hats, and these are no longer knotted lancer- wise. Clusters of short tips stand up at the side of broad-brimmed sailors. Circles of the same trim toques and turbans and other diminutive chapeaux, whilst short tips stand out at inter- vals from the crowns of some small hats in a bizarre fashion that has little to commend it, from an artistic point of view. Feather fans have been much in evidence of late, either in black, or white, or bOth. They are large in, size, and so soft and pretty, they deserve to be always in fashion. Ostrich feathers have for the moment replaced the aigrette that has been so long worn as an ornament in the evening coiffure.

Colour in Sunshades. When buying sunshades that are required to protect the face \ from the effect of the sun's rays, it is well to bear in mind that black is practically useless for that purpose. Blue, also, gives scarcely any protection, because it keeils out only those sun's rays that are not harmful, whilst it admits those that tan the skin, and produce 'sun headaches. Green, combined with yellowish brown, gives the best Shade, and light brown tussore lined with green, or white also lined with green, make the best sunshades for all practical purposes. Red also is to be recom- mended, especially when lined with white, and green is effectual even when there is no lining.

div.head: COOKERY CORNER. A Couple of Niee Dishes.
div.p: COOKERY CORNER. A Couple of Niee Dishes.

Hampshire pudding is a useful dish, made thus: Finely shred 40z. beef suet (previously baked and having got cold), mix it into 12oz. of self-raising flour. Top and tail and wash, and drain a pint of gooseberries. Stir them with the suet and flour. Beat up an egg with a little milk; and mix all, to a stiff paste consistently. Dip a cloth through boiling water, wring dry, turn the mixture into the cloth, tie, and plunge into fast boiling water. Boil fast five minutes, then gently two hours. Serve hot with simple sweet sauce and sugar. This is, nice made with both green and. ripe berries. , For the latter serve hot with cream and sugar, or home-made "Devonshire Cream?' • Cod Stuffed and Baked.

This is a nice light dish to take the place of beef on a hot day. Take a,small cod, about 21b. weight. Clean it, scrape well, and do not leave any blood on the bone. .Mix 4 tablespoonfuls breadcrumbs, 11. tablespoonfuls chopped suet, 1 dessertspoonful chopped parsley, Pepper and , salt all together. Add enough milk to moisten. Put this into the fish, and sew it up. Run a trussing needle threaded with linen thread through the tail, the centre of the body, and the head. Pull and tie the thread; this draws the fish into the shape of the letter S. Score the fish on the sides, and press a narrow strip of fat pork into the spaces. Brush over with milk and dust some crumbs on top. Put some drip- ping into a deep tin. Bake, allowing ten minutes to each pound, and ten minutes over, basting frequently. Take it up. Remove trussing strings, and slip on to a hot dish. Garnish with parsley and slices of lemon. Serve with parsley sauce NM\

div.head: WORLD.
div.p: WORLD.
CHAT and GOSSIP.
By MARJORIE.
The Kaiser's Grandsons.

It is curious to note how boys predominate in the German Imperial family. The German Emperor, who has only one brother, is the father of six sons and one daughter. The Crown Prince has four sons and no daughter, and in the other families of the Kaiser's married sons there are more princes than princesses. The children of the German Crown Prince and Princess are growing up very quickly, or so it seems to their elders. The second in succession to the German Emperor is, of course, the eldest son of the Crown Prince, who is now eight years old; the youngest is three. The Kaiser super- intends the education of his grandsons, and like all German princes, they are brought up on Spartan lines. They spend the greater part of each day in the open air, and are taught to ride almost as soon as they can walk.

The Revival of Needlecraft. It is satisfactory to note that a revival in needlecraft has set in. The perfecting of the sewing machine and the great improvement in factory-made embroideries and lace led to the utter neglect of needlework by the women of the latter part of Queen Victoria's reign. Needle- work, more especially the rarer kinds, was, in fact, in danger of becoming a lost art, but was rescued from oblivion by the Royal School at Kensington, and similar institutions in other parts of the country. Fashion, like history, re- peats itself, and now it is fashionable to be in- terested in needlework, more especially in the , newer kinds, and these are legion. Quaint specimens of old work regarded as rubbish in the seventies, are now brought out from cup- boards and chests, and carefully studied and copied, while handmade embroideries and laces are the occupations of leisure hours and are seen in fashionable drawing-rooms. Tub Frocks.
Washing frocks were never prettier than this year. They are simple, too, and practical, as they should be, when their laundering has to be

considered. The fabrics from which they are made are light and charming, and their colour- ing most beautiful. The floral and other de.- signs are delightful, and combine excellently with the plain materials. Spotted cottons and foulards are always worn more or less, the difference in each season being the size of the spot, and the favourite colouring. Years ago blue grounds and white spots were very popu- lar, and bright blue is favoured this year. Deep red with large white spots is considered very smart this summer, and is certainly bright look- ing. For more elaborate frocks, tussore silk is in high favour again, and fancy coats of the spotted material, with the plain tussore for skirts, are among the most effective and dressy costumes. The collars, cuffs, sashes or bands, and vests match the spots in colour. Stripes always look well in cotton materials, and re- quire no trimming beyond lingerie or pique collars and waistcoats. The Lace Scarf. _ .

_ The tunic is an important feature of the cotton frock, as is also the waistcoat, and with the aid of these accessories the middle-aged woman may indulge in the prettiest of cotton frocks, which moreover are quite suitable to her appearance, and may be depended upon to give a youthful effect. In many cases both tunic and waistcoat are simulated, or the latter is cut in one with the collar, and made separately from the dress, which is a sensible idea for cotton frocks that require washing. The lace scarf never goes really out of fashion; it is too ele- gant and beautiful not to find admirers and patrons, but this year it will have an unusual vogue. The finest specimens are, of course, handworked, but these are necessarily very ex- pensive, and manufacturers have become so ex- pert in making the most exact imitations of all the beautiful old laces that handsome scarves are within the reach of the woman of the most moderate means. Lace fichus are also to be worn, and those fortunate erlough to possess real old lace can utilise it with het, or the stronger makes of tulle, for either of these charming accessories.

The Lace Hat and the Sash. The lace hat, whether in black or white—and one is as popular as the other—is of the larger type, with most becoming lines. Tate de negre is quite a favourite shade for hats, whilst bleached white, and _ivory in its purity, are popular also, and most suitable for girls blessed

div.head: HINTS ON HEALTH. Need of Refreshing Sleep.
div.p: HINTS ON HEALTH. Need of Refreshing Sleep.

A refreshing night's sleep is almost an im- possibility if the bed has been carelessly or improperly made, and one rises in the morning unfit for the day's duties, no matter what form The occupation takes. To a tired worker it is an absolute luxury to lie on a cool, comfortable bed, with just the correct amount of clothing, and each article properly arranged. To ensure a good night's rest, the bed must be stripped of all covering; the sheets and blankets being spread one at a time over a couple of chairs, and the pillows being shaken and placed where plenty of air can pass over them.

Art of Bed-making. - The window should be left open; and the bed not made for at least an hour; then proceed in this way: Put on the under sheet, and turn it well under at the head—quite a foot, for it is from this end thaethe strain on the lower sheet comes, while the strain on the clothes over the sleeper comes from the foot of the bed. There- fore remember that the lower sheet, must be made secure at the head, and the coverings well tucked in at the foot. Tuck in each article, as, you put it on the bed, along the sides and at the foot, and if extra warmth is required over the feet, place a folded blanket over that part of the bed, tucking it under at the foot and the sides. If an under blanket is desired this should be placed on the bed first, before the under sheet, and secured like the latter at the head.

Attend to the Teeth. Attend to your children's teeth. Decayed teeth and a poisoned mouth are responsible for nine- tenths of those intestinal and digestive troubles that -cause terrible suffering in after-life.

div.head: MEMS. FOR MOTHERS. How Long Should a Child Sleep?
div.p: MEMS. FOR MOTHERS. How Long Should a Child Sleep?

As a general rule, it may be taken that the younger a child is the more sleep it requires. As children need a greater amount of sleep than adults, so a child of five months old needs more than one of five or six years. This may be ex- plained by the fact that the development of consciousness moves parallel with the increase of age, and the weaker the consciousness the more easily the organism •is exhausted. Thus in the case of infants at the breast the con- sciousness is so feebly developed that a very short time of wakefulness will exhaust them. The practice, very common among nurses and servants, of allowing young children to sleep as long as possible—frequently for the selfish reason that while a child sleeps it is giving them no trouble—is, however, directly harmful. Eight Hours at Least. Since consciousness, like every other function, requires exercise for its proper development, it is evident that the mind of a child which sleeps for an undue proportion of its time will develop proportionately slowly. For the first five or six months a child should be awake for about two hours during the day, and this period should increase as the child grows old.r. From one or two years old children should have 16 or 18 hours of sleep out of the 24'; from two to three, 15 or 17 hours; between three and four, 14 to 16 hours; between four and six, 13 to 15 hours; between Band nine, 10 to 12 hours; and between nine and 13 years, from eight to ten hours. Only when the growth is complete, at about 19 or 20, can the amount of sleep be brought safely as low as six or eight hours a day: On the whole, eight hours is on the average the best amount of sleep for healthy adults.

Christ appeared to His disciples He rebuked their want of faith. Evidently He meant to imply that in company with Him, and faith in Him, there could be no disaster, There was a time coming when the self-same disciples would face the prospects of a more horrible death than drowning at sea. without one word of complaint and without even the.shadow of distrust.

boy, whose father was aboard the ill-fated liner as one of the "Black Squad," led him to ex- amine the lists. The boy lcioked for his father's name in vain. There was no account of him in the list of the saved, and the brave man turned away with a sigh, murmuring " God's : will be done !" That blind sailor had not reached such a robust patience without a fiery trial; and in human life we discover that God cares in the very way in which He perfects our character. Faith in God, and, in the midst of disaster, a rooted belief that God does care, was manifested by the Christians aboard. The Sal- vation Army officers added a dignity to their order, and honour to their God, as they faced death murmuring of a faith that will not shrink; when they joined in saying " God be with you till we meet again." ven the most practical of men must confess that this plain life is shrouded in mystery, and though they may boast of their prac- tical methods, there is little doubt that about us and around us is a wonderful mystery, that no practical business man can fathom. In these moments of sadness, a bard, limited view of human life is of no avail. That attitude cannot avert the disaster now it is past, nor console those who are suffering. But now we have a full list of the dead. And in this memorial service I we can say that there is a sure and certain hope of a resurrection in Christ Jesus. The fathom- lelts sea cannot imprison a soul, and we are as near resurrection in a sailor's grave as in the handsome mausoleum of a, king. One rejoices in the Christian spirit of the whole nation in her efforts to meet the physical needs of the mourning and the suffering; and it is but just and true to say that the expression of pity, coupled with the practical hand of assistance from a whole nation, rightly mani- fests that God does care, and that He cares lest we perish!

During the service several appropriate hymns were sung and prayers offered. The former in- cluded "God moves in a mysterious way," "Eternal Father, strong to save," and "0 God, our help in ages past."

div.head: Nature Demands Oare.
div.p: Nature Demands Oare.

Does God care whether men perish or nay? A cool scepticism will say that because a thousand have perished in a recent disaster, there can be no humane God controlling the affairs of this life. One is not deeply concerned ;with the idle speculations of scepticism, but there are those whose very grief is poignant, and they will ask if there be a God. When one surveys human life, there is much of it that appears like a human shambles. One hymn-writer puts it that "the world is full of sighs, full of sad and weeping eyes," and then adds, " Oh ! the good we all may do while the days are going by." If every man was as good and as careful as he could be, there would be less sad and weeping eyes; and the cruelty and carelessness of men cannot by any stretch of argument indict God. Does God care? Could God have averted the disaster of the Titanic? Lord Mersey, in his summing up., as chairman of the Commission, declared there was excessive speed. We should pity rather than blame the brave captain who per- ished; but in the economy of this world God has not schemed to avert the disasters of human carelessness or human errors. A thousand mortals were lost at the mouth of the St. Lawrence. Suppose God had lifted the vapoury mist, or suppose that He had stayed the hands of the captain; and yet the human works so much destruction; the fact that somebody blundered is no argument against God. Then Nature reminds us that she cannot be treated save with the utmost care. One has watched the oiler of an engine move with wild daring amongst its wheels and cranks. One moment of thoughtlessness or carelessness and the mangled remains relate the result. Nature de- mands just, continuous and strenuous care. There are features about Nature that remind us she is still unconquered. Hamel had toyed with the air until lie seemed her master; there was one journey and now after it a long silence. Nature grimly asserted her mastery. The Alps have a knack, in spite of all man's triumphs, of revealing they are still unconquered. A party reach to the land of its immense silences, there is a rumble and a rush, and the plateau on which they were last seen is absolutely clear. In these days it is said the last word in ship- building has been spoken, and yet in fifteen minutes one of the crack liners lies in fifteen fathoms. The majesty of Nature's greatness should lead men to reverence its Author and its Maker. And over the watery grave of the dead, we can say that God holds the keys to all the unknown/

In a Wonderful Way. And yet God does care, and cares in a wonder- ful way! The disciples who said " Carest thou not that we perish?" were preserved to face a more fearful end. The day came when they faced the stake, and suffered martyrdom with a brave patience. Here in the narrative we see them childishly petulant.. There came a day when they were robustly patient. div.head: PRACTICAL PRESCRIPTION AGAINST STOMACH ACIDITY.
div.p: PRACTICAL PRESCRIPTION AGAINST STOMACH ACIDITY.
BY A SPECIALIST.

"Nine-tenths of all cases of stomach trouble nowadays," says a leading specialist, "are caused by too much acid In the beginning the stomach itself is not diseased, but if this acid condition is allowed to continue, the acid is very likely to eat into the stomach walls and pro• duce stomach ulcer or cancer,_either of which may render a radical surgical operation neces- sary, even to prolong life. Therefore an 'acid stomach' is really a dangerous condition and should be treated seriously. It is utterly useless to take pepsin and ordinary stomach tablets. The excess acid must be neutralised by the ad- ' ministration of an efficient antacid. For this purpose physicians nearly always recommend taking half a teaspoonful of bisurated magnesia in a little water after each meal. Larger quan- tities may be used if necessary, as it is abso- lutely harmless. But be sure to get the bisur- ated magnesia, as other forms of magnesia have not the same action hi the stomach as the bisur- ated, and frequently *do more harm than good."

div.p: A QUAINT NAME.

..... • Aunt Lindy had brought around her three grandchildren for/ her mistress to see. The three little darkies, in calico smocks, stood squirming n line while Lindy proudly surveyed them. " What are their names, Lindy?" her Mistress asked. ' "Dey's name' after flowers, ma'am. Ah name' 'em. De bigges' one's name' Gladiola. Do flex' one, she name' Heliotrope."
