THE CAT WAITER. Because of his fidelity to Harry of Richmond —afterwards Henry Vll.—Sir Henry Wyat was imprisoned in the Tower of London by Richard 111. One day, while he was in confinement, a cat came to him. He petted her, and, crumbling bread in water, offered her something to eat. After this she visited him every day, occasion- ally bringing him a pigeon. He complained to his keeper of his cold and scanty rations, and that official said he dared not change the bill of fare.
"If I will provide any fowl, will you dress and cook it for me?" asked the prisoner. "I can safely promise you that," was the reply.
Consequently such pigeons as the cat brought Sir Henry were dressed and cooked for him. .

When on the crowning of the one he had served so well, Sir Henry was released, he had painted a picture of the cat with a pigeon in her claws offering it to him through a grated window. To this day the picture is preserved in a collection of historical paintings that may he seen in London.

div.head: STORY OF PINS.
div.p: THE STORY OF PINS.

. . - Once beyond the stark naked stage, it is hard to imagine a state of human society in which pins were not a daily necessity. And a little investigation will show that, as a matter of fact, the harmless, necessary pin is of very great antiquity indeed. Whatever literature you look into, no matter how ancient or rudi- mentary, you will come across references to the pin. Pins of wood and bone and ivory, pins of bronze and of gold and silver—all these were known to and used by the ancient Egyptians and the Babylonians, by Greeks, and Romans, and Jews. The common pin of brass is mentioned early in the Old Testament—in the book of Exodus, to be exact. China knew and used the pin when our fathers and mothers were running

ANNUAL PRIZE DISTRIBUTION.

There was a good attendance at Orford Hall on Saturday afternoon, when Professor Bompas Smith, Professor of Education at Manchester University-, attended to present prizes won by the students. The Rev. Canon Morley Steven- son presided, and amongst others present were : Professor Campagnac, Professor of EdueaZiot and Dean of the Faculty of Arts of Liverpool: University; Rev. G. Vale Owen, Rev. W. Heady Cock, Dr. Bowden, college medical officer; Mr. ' W. Mason, master of method; Miss M. Brown,' lady superintendent; Miss Steel, resident gov- erness, and Miss Brown, a former lady superin- tendent. A number of relatives and friends of the students also attended.

div.head: UNIQUE POSITION OF THE COLLEGE.
div.p: UNIQUE POSITION OF THE COLLEGE.

The Rey. Canon Morley Stevenson said that Was the only college of its kind in England, and was entirely intended for those who were tech- nically called certificated students—for those who had been teaching in the schools for some time and thought they would like a further year of study and training. Of course, certificated students were received in many other colleges throughout the country, but that was the only one entirely devoted to that class of student, and therefore they would obviously see the gain to be derived. During the year those who had been in the college had been a most earnest band of students, who had tried to utilise to the full all its advantages. They had been eager in look- ing out for new methods of teaching and any- thing new in school life and work, and so bring- ing themselves up to date as much as possible. (Applause.) They were very much indebted to Mr. Mason, the master of method, and also to Miss Brown and Miss Steel, who had worked so , faithfully. They had a larger number .of stu- dents this year than last, when they sank to a very small number, and he hoped that next year they would reach the maximum of 30. He was quite certain that as the college became better known and understood they would not be lack- ing for students. (Applause.)

THE THEORETICAL SIDE OF TEACHING. Professor Smith, after presenting the prizes, said he was honoured by being asked to attend, especially because it was a college in which the students were not the ordinary type of students, but teachers who, in the midst of their teach- ing life, had given a year to further study. He hoped that institutions of that kind would mul- tiply in numbers: (Applause.), It seemed to him that the interest in the more theoretical side of teaching was becoming so widespread that in the future further opportunities ought to be offered and taken 'advantage of; they looked upon that college setting an example to the country. Whether it was followed or not was 'not their business. They were proud to have a part, however small, in a college of that kind. (Applause.) They should agree that a year of such training was not so much a thing ' complete in itself, but the beginning of another ia clues teachi:lg 1,44, that, gave, a aew

div.head: RED CROSS NURSES.
div.p: RED CROSS NURSES.
Sham Fight__ at Grappenhall
A VALUABLE INSTITUTION.

General excitement prevailed in Grappenhall on Saturday, when the usual calm of the village was disturbed by the sound of firing and loud battle cries. The occasion was the annual in- spection of the Daresbury Division Voluntary Aid Detachments (Chesbires 22 and 48) of the British Red Cross Society. The local battalion of the Church Lads' Brigade, commanded by Lieut.-Colonel Appleton, held a sham fight in the park adjoining Grappenhall Hall (by Or- mission of Mr. F. Aylmer Frost), and supplied casualties for treatment by the Red Cross nurses. A large number visited the village to witness the manceuvres and to inspect the hos- pitals.

The general idea of the fight was that Lanca- shire and Cheshire, being two separate and independent states, were at war, and that on Friday a severe action had taken place for the possession of the bridges over the Ship Canal at Latchford. After a struggle, Cheshire had been repulsed in some confusion, the bridges re- maining in Lancashite's possession. Accord- ingly, Cheshire retired through Grappenhall village towards Knutsford, and "blew up" Grappenhall bridge. .They were, however, un- successful in their attempt to blow up Stanny Lunt bridge. At the same time, the Lancashire troops were , too fatigued to pursue the enemy far, and Che- shire went into bivouac at Appleton Thorn, covered by outposts, a fresh battalion of Lanca- shire infantry reaching Warrington at noon on Saturday. _ _ _ _

The Lancashire forces were commanded by Captain Henshall, with the assistance of Lieizts. Bottomley and Isherwood, and the Cheshire forces by Sergtvlnstructor Howells. Lieut.- Colonel Appleton, Major Brookes, Capt. Sankey and Lieut. Frost (4th Battalion) , acted as um- pires, and the St. Paul's and St. Elphin's ambu- lance' companies were present under Instructor Gibson. Stretchers were lent by the Warring- ton police and Messrs. Peter Walker and Son, Ltd.

Two companies of the 2nd Liverpool cadet battalion:, under Captain Henshall; advanced from Warrington early in the afternoon, driv- ing back the enemy's rearguard on to their main body, still considerably disorganised from Friday's severe action. Previously, Captain Henshall had despatched all available cyclists to seize and hold Stanny Lunt bridge. These cyclists drove back all the enemy they encoun- tered, until the Captain had got possession of the bridge with his infantry.

div.head: AMBULANCE WORK.
div.p: AMBULANCE WORK.

The British Red Cross Society nurses occupied the neutral hospitals established at the school (surgical and medical wards, operating theatre, bathrooms and laundry), the Hull billiard-room and the Parish Room (isolation hospital). The Cheshire 22 detachment was in the command of Afiss M. Broadbent; Nurse Callender, lady superintendent; Mrs. Frost, quartermaster; and Mrs. Bower, head cook. There were three other cooks, one laundress, and sixteen nurses. Col. Averill, county director, was also present. The Cheshire 48 detachment was commanded by Miss Monks; Mrs. Gordon Roberts was quar- termaster; and Nurse Wherritt, lady superin- tendent; whilst the infectious diseases hospital was in the charge of Mrs. Turner and Miss Ronald, Miss E. Evans acting as cook.

div.head: CHESHIRE EFFICIENCY.
div.p: CHESHIRE EFFICIENCY.

Colonel Clarke, of Chester, acted as inspecting officer, and in the evening addressed the assem- bled nurses, of whom there were 36. He said that the excellent standard in Cheshire was keeping up the high reputation. which the eounty had already gained. When the nurses donned the uniform of the society, they must take on its responsibility. They must have keenriess and efficiency, 'learn immediately to treat accidents, and add hygiene to their reper- toire of accomplishments. They should also learn the rights and privileges to which they were entitled.
Colonel Averill proposed a hearty vote of thanks to Mr. and Mrs. Frost for allowing them the use of their park and part of the hall. The Red Cross Society, he said, was greatly indebted to them.
, The motion was carried with acclamation.

In reply, Mr. Frost said it had given Mrs. Frost and him very great pleasure to,help them; they difl it most willingly. He trusted that the Society would become well established in the country, and to make it so, its Members must not wait till their services were required, but be- come efficient straight away. Miss Sylvia Broadbent, secretary of the Society, thanked Colonel Clarke for his thorough inspection. After tea, which was provided at the hall for visitors at a nominal charge, the St. Paul's Bugle Band played several marches in front of the hall and concluded with the retreat beating.

It ap- plied to a teacher who could manage a class with skill, that skill which came from experi- ence, but that was of no use if it was not based upon knowledge. (Applause.) Professor Campagnac proposed, and the Rev. W. Heady Cock seconded, a vote of thanks to the speakers, which was heartily carried.

WAR MEDALS FOR HUNGARIAN WOMEN.

The 'war medal of 1912-13 has been awarded to all who performed military duties on the frontier, and as in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the postal and telegraph services are under military control, their employes are also eligible, so that we have the somewhat rare event of several women workers who operated the telephone at Serajevo being decorated with war medals.

PRIZE DISTRIBUTION.

Mr. R. H. Raiford announced the results amidst loud applause, and congratulated the winners on the splendid fight they had made. To attain such an honour was no trifling matter. Both teams had played exceedingly well throughout the competition. They were very pleased the final had come about • in such a con- clusive manner, although they would have liked the watches to have been scattered in different parts of the town. They were keenly, engaged in political work as well as recreation, and he hoped they would put the same energy in the former as in the latter, and return Mr. Crosfleld at the next election, for at present they felt they were not properly represented. If they re- turned Mr: Crosfield they would feel that a good sound work had been done. (Applause.) MRS. PARKER AND OUR "CHAMPION" MAYOR.
Afrs Parker then made the presentation, con- gratulated the winning team, and wished Orford more success in the future. (Applause.) -

Mr. E. E. Hughes proposed a vote of thanks to Mrs. Parker, and sala they could not have a better lady to present the prizes. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Litton seconded; and Mr. Parker, in sup- porting, said Mrs. Parker had not what every bowl had—a bias. (Laughter.) It was a good thing to be absolutely without bias in every- thing except bowls. (Hear, hear.)

. - • In reply, Mrs. Parker said that the play had been of a very interesting' character, and not all from the winners either. Personally, her bias, if she had any, would be for the losing side, for she would like to have oen a new name on the cup. (hear,, hear.) No. one appreciated mom than she had done the kindness of the Mayor in giving that trophy. _ They had a champion and She was of the opinion. that no one IMmadyo Lie more than he for the working people. She thanked them cordially for their very kind reception. (Applause.) NICE-PRESIDENTS' MAIN.

div.head: SATURDAY, JUNE 27,
div.p: SATURDAY, JUNE 27,
CRICKET.
WARRINGTON'S FINE FORM.
Good Matches Between Local Clubs.

The Warrington senior team were again in fine form when they were entertained by the Cheetham eleven on Saturday. Batting first, the Warringtonians were soon making an acceptable score, and when they aggregated 239 for the loss of nine wickets they deemed it wise to declare. However, the remaining time was not sufficient. to dispose of the•home team, who for the loss of five wickets made 120 runs. W. Richardson, for Warrington, knocked 79 to- gether in masterly fashion and had the satis- faction of being the highest scorer. Warring- ton's next best batsman was S. Baxter, who successfully defied the opposition and scored 41, a single short of F. J. Smethurst's total, which constituted the Cheetham team's highest num- ber. S. L. Partridge was out lbw for 29, whilst G. Woodcock and B. Si'cock ceased to trouble the scorers when they had made 28. The Warrington professional secured the fire Cheetbam wickets at the cost of 65 runs.

Sankey were in merry form on Saturday, when, after. dismissing Rough Green for the meagre score of 20, they compiled 67, and then had lost eight wickets. Sankey's bowling was very good, Forster obtaining five wickets for seven runs, and Millington four for nine runs.

Rylands' Recreation made a poor stand on Saturday against their visitors, the Runcorn .11.F.C. team. The Runcorn eleven mustered 70, against the local team's 36, and there were no less than six "ducks" amongst the Recreation's players.

In a game at Appleton on Saturday between Stockton Heath and Cairo-street Unitarians, the latter were losers by .four runs. The Uni- tarians batted first and compiled 39, the highest scorer being R. Williams, Who mustered 10. The " Heathens" opened badly, but with ,the 'aid of A. Johnson's' 18 they were responsible for 43 runs, which gave them the victory.

At Grappenhall on Saturday the village team entertained Oughtrington and suffered defeat at their hands. Batting first, the visitors Chiefly through the instrumentality of F. Champ (23) and N. Wood (13), made 61 runs. Grappenhall replied with 58, J. Ford (15) being their highest scorer. OF '

. By reason of their home victory over Padgate Wesleyans on Saturday, Orford Juniors have strengthened their position in the Warrington and Diftriet Junior League. For the winners, Ashton 117) and Hollowa (10) were the chief contributors to an aggregate of 54 .runs, whilst the Wesleyans' 29 runs were made by Rowland (10), Chantler (7), and Gleave (6), whilst extras accounted to/ the further runs.

The Working Men's Mission visited Elmwood Avenue Congregationalists on Saturday, And for the loss of liMe wickets secured exactly double the 'total 'runs of their opponents T. O'Neil and ock'. Appleton both garnered 14 runs, whilst Ecclestom with ten, was the next bight scorer for the visitors. The Congregationalists compiled 39, to which James Plnenix contri- buted 11 and J. Pritchard 10. For the Mission, J. McGarr took eight wickets for 11 runs.

Bold-street Wesleyans secured their fifth suc- cessive victory by defeating Cairo-strcet Uni- tarians (2nd eleven), on the ground of the latter, by 37 runs. Tlie Wesleyans' total was 56; due mainly to the bdtting, of W. W. Westwell (17) and D. B. Weaver (13 not out). Cairo-street could do very little against the bowling of the Wesleynns, Stringer taking, 5 wickets for 4 runs, and Cooper 4 for 9, and had only scored 19 when their •last wicket fell. W. Cooper did the "hat trick"- for Bold-street, who will meet Rylands' _Rees.' reserve at home to-day.

div.head: WARRINGTON BEAT SOUTHPORT.
div.p: WARRINGTON BEAT SOUTHPORT.

In the first round for the Ijan-eashire Junior Cup Warrington met Southport in the local baths on Tuesday evening. There wka:* an ea- ceedinglyf large attendance and the teams turned out as follows:— Warrington—C. Wood; L. Graham and S. Tare; C. Turner (Captain), 11. Si 6E3072, J. Graham, and It Pepper._
South port—.T.unip;"....T. -B. Hughes and A, B. Bebbington; C. Dix, Jr. Marshall, P. Peet, and. J. Box.
• _ The referee was Mr. J. Gomersall, cf-Evertori.
THE GAME.

Warrington were by far the bettei team, ant, defending the shallow end, soon bombarded the opposite goal. ,The visitors had few chances, and these they missed through very we:tk shooting. Pepper and -Turner played remailc• ably well, hut they had hard lines with smac good .shots. After about one minute's pl..y Pepper opened Warrington's account with a stinging shot, and ;scored again before tho interval. Sonthport seemed to be 'warming up," but their efforts proved futile. In the second half Warrington again rue- called, goals being added by Pepper i,nd Tur• ner. The visitors tried to fore* -matteis, but. they were repeatedly brought up for breach,* of the rules. Peet was their only scorer; and. he put two very neat ones. through the stielf:7. The final came with the score: Warrington, 4; Southport, 2.

TANNERS' STRIKE.
NO SETTLEMENT YET IN SIGHT.
The strike still continues.

In reply to -a-letieTi;;;-The Masters' Federa- tion, asking whether the Union were prepared to admit that the stri-ke was official, the Union officials state the cause of the strike could only .be explained by the delay in treating the griev- ances of the men by the Conciliation Board. In addition, the men assumed that preparations for a lock-out were•being made by the employers by shortening the input of bides in the pits. Since, however, the strike was complete, no use- ful purpose could be served by unduly prolong- ing the negotiations, and therefore, they sug- gested a conference should be convened at an early date, when ways and means of a settle- ment could be devised.
This reply will be considered by the masters at their Meeting on Monday.

ARBITRATORS ASK FOR INSTRUCTIONS. We have received from the chairman of the Conciliation Board of the Warrington, Runcorn, and District Master Tanners' Association and the Tanners' Union, a copy of the following ruling of the arbitrators in relation to a matter submitted to them by that Board : " According to the instructions received from the secretary of the Conciliation Board of the Warrington, Runcorn, and District Master-Tan- ners' 'association and the Tanners' Union, we, the undersigned, met together on June 3rd at the office of Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons. "Your Secretary, Mr. Mitchell, laid before us the resolution upon which you desired us to arbitrate, viz.: 'Whether South American hides are included under the 'agreement for fleshing rates.' Mr. Mitchell gave us the history of the negotiations up to date, and from that history it appears that since the question in dis- , pute left the Conciliation Board • and was re- ferred to us, the men have taken the law into their own hands by declaring a strike. I "Under these circumstances, we do not feel that we have any warrant for arbitration, and beg to refer the matter back again to the Con- ciliation Board to learn their further wishes on the matter. "(Signed), „
"GEORGE CROSFIELD. " JAMF,S SEXTON." STATEMENT BY THE SECRETARY OF THE MASTERS' ASSOCIATION.

With reference to the interview with Mr. Ormsby, general secretary to the Tanners' Union, reported in the "Daily Citizen" of June 24th, the Master Tanners' Association would like to correct some of the statements. _ _

Mr. Ormsby was reported as saying: When we drew the attention of the employers to the possibility of trouble, owing to the presence of two non-union men at one yard, they said they could not interfere. Immediately following that, the employers posted lock-out notices." No lock-out notices were posted, but the masters said that lock-out notices would be posted if the strike notice on that point was not withdrawn. As, article 20 in the agreement of September 29th states: " The masters cannot agree to make any distinction between union and non-union men in the works." The -Union had no right to .take the action which Mr. Ormsby says they. took. Fleshing South American hides. Mr. Ormsby states that " The price means a reduction of id. per hide to the men." . The price represented in some Tanyards a small advance; in some a small reduction; and on the prices paid before the September agree- ment, very few men are affected. Taking fleshers as a whole, I should hay that the price paid for fleshing South American hides is a slight ad- vance on the prices paid previously. As to other statements. the whole agreement was published in your columns last week. (Signed)
C. H. MITCHELL, Secretary Master Tanners' Association. A WORD FOR THE MEN. , To the Editor of "The Examiner."

...... Sir,—The position that Mr. D. A. Thomas holds in the South Wales coalfield also applies to Mr. C. E. Parker of the tanning industry in this district. The characteristics of the two gentlemen vary very little. Of the two, Mr. Parker, I should consider, from his articles in the Press, to be the most democratic. He is now put to the test, and ivorking men will have an opportunity of proving whether he is their friend or not.

Apart from the beamsmen's grievance, I con- sider it a shame that a tannery labourer should put in 12 months' probation before he is entitled to the munificent sum of 51d. per hour. Give him a minimum of 61. per hour, and abolish the probationary system. Every labourer is worthy of his hire. If he is not, his services eah be dispensed with. The extra halfnenny per hour (and what is it?) means all the difference in the world to him. It will give him a chance of better food, better clothes, and the opportunity of putting a little by for a rainy day. It is 'in the power of Mr. Parker to make the men's position happier, and no doubt he will do his best for the men and their wives and Our last labour dispute was not worth the cost and suffering which it entailed, but the tanners have a real grievance, and should be supported. CHESHIRE IN LONDON. Inaugural Meeting of County Association. As it is computed that there are about 8,000 natives of Cheshire in London, there should be little difficulty in obtaining a large member- ship to the new Cheshire Society, which was inaugurated at a meeting at the Holborn Restaurant, London, on Monday. Through the formation of this new society, there are now only four counties which cannot boast of a united body of their county men in the capital of the Empire. Major Louis A. Newton pre- sided. "A Good Level County." The Rev. Dr. Caldeeott, of King'a"College, said

that the fuAtion of the County Association was to keep alive what the French called "regional feelings" in their composite nation. In a recent public discussion on which county had produced the greatest men, Lancashire was given the first place, but, said -Dr. Caldecott, while Cheshire had not produced the giants of English life, she had produced her full share in the "middle levels." Good solid Cheshire names were known in every department of English life. Cheshire was, perhaps, too rich and pleasant a part of God's earth for its people to have made those tremendous efforts necessary for genius, but they could congratulate themselves that they came from a part of England favoured by Nature, well cultivated by man, and with a uniformly high level of human life. Cheshire was indeed "a good level county." Cheshire Characteristics. Mr. Gershon' Stewart, M.P., in some amusing references to the county's history, gave a monk's description of Cheshire folk as "very sociable in their entertainment, cheerful at meals—not given to excess in eating—fond of borrowing other people's property." (Laughter.) The Duke of Westminster was elected the first president, and amongst the vice-presidents are Mr. Horatio Lloyd, Mr., J. L. Garvin, Mr. Mallaby Deeley, Sir Alfred Smith and Mr. F. E. Smith. Tb- Society is affiliated to the Conference of EnglL.t County Societies. _ RUNCORN GUARDIANS' ELECTION. Polling took place on Saturday in Newtown Ward, Runcorn, for a representative on the' Runcorn Board of Guardians. Less than 20 per cent, of the electors took the trouble to vote. The question of the future of the Grammar School was dealt with somewhat fully, on the initiation of the School Management Com- mittee, at the Education Committee, which met on Monday, Councillor H. Roberts pre- siding. The subject was given a full-dress discussion, but, as Canon Stevenson aptly put it, they were moving in a clouded atmosphere, as they had not the whole facts and figures before them. It was pointed out that before any- thing drastic was done there should be a friendly conference between the parties. The Committee submitted a report of a con- ference with the Board of Education with respect to the proposals of the governors, and the relation thereof to the general provision of secondary education in the borough.

We estimate that there dre not 200 boys in Warrington,' or ,'anything Like that number, whose fathers can pay the existing fees at the drammar School, so that if the school is to re- ceive 200 scholars there must be a reduction in the fee to attract boys. That means a lessen- ing of the income, and we should have larger charges for maintenance. We have figures which we cannot print in the minutes at the moment. These figures are confidentially sup- plied-to us by -the Board of Education. if the committee resolves itself into a General Pur- poses Committee, the Chairman will probably give these figures. We have estimated, as closely as we can, that this income will fall far short of what the governors have anticipated, because of the existence of lower fees, greater cost of main- tenance and loss in other ways. We look for- ward to being asked to contribute not only .t4OO, but considerably more, because if there is a de- ficit, to whom will the governors of the Gram- mar School go? To the ratepayers. We believe this money is insufficient, and that we shall have to find from the rates a great deal more. WORKIJIGMEN'S COMMITTEES. The Mayor Entertains Workers for Infirmary and Nursing Association.

The Mayor and Mayoress (Councillor .and Mrs. Peter Peacock) held a reception at the Town Hall on Saturday afternoon, to which the members of the Working Men's Infirmary Com- mittee and the Working Men's Committee of the District Nursing Association and their wives or lady friends were invited. - There was a large response, and, in spite of the brief thunderstorm which threatened to mar the occasion, but fortunately gave way to pleas- ant conditions, a most enjoyable afternoon was spent. The Mayor and Mayoress received their guests in the Council Chamber, which was tastefully decorated witl growing plants, and the gardens, which were closed to the public, made a delight- ful promenade, and for nearly three hours pre- sented an animated and happy-looking picture. Mr. Boothroyd's band played in the grounds, and afterwards in the vestibule of the Town Hall, and Mr. and Mrs. Mitchell provided first-

• tended a welcome to his guests, and he and the Mayoress were thanked for their kindness, his Worship, at the request of Mr. George Walker, vice-chairman of the committee, presented Alderman Burton with a handsome solid silver fruit stand, supplied by Messrs. LIBERAL BOWLERS. St. Austin's Win the "Peacock Cup." A GREAT FINAL. • Worl,ers in the ranks of Liberalism are well provided for as regards recreation. One of the most popular competitions in which members of the various wards take part is that for the "Peter Peacock" Challenge Cup, given to the best team of bowlers. For many weeks past the greatest enthusiasm and keenest, but friendly, rivalry,.ha,s prevailed on the Bank Quay bowling green, wbeie the numerous teams have struggled in real sportsmanlike fashion for supremacy. ~The final stage of the competition on Saturday was interfered with to a certain extent by two or three showers, but the play both in the semi- nal and filial was of the usual high standard. Praise is due to the officials, whose admirable arrangements have been largely responsible for the success of this great competition. Mrs. C. E. Parker, who was accompanied by Mr. C. E. Parker, president of the Liberal Association, presented the cup and gold watches to the win- ners—St. Austin's D team—and the gun metal watches to the runners-up, Orford A tcam. The Mayor was not present in deference to his deci- sion not to know any politics during his year of office. THE SCORES. In the following details of the semi-final the

one point, after a very strenuous game. Mr. Joseph Wilkinson, chairman of the bowl- ing club, presented the prizes, and congratulated the successful players on their achievements. As he was the winner of the fourth prize, Mr. J. T. Smith; vice-chairman of the bowling club, banded the Chairman his prize amidst loud cheers. All the vice-presidents of the club had contri- buted to the prizes, and they were heartily ,thanked for their generosity, on the proposition of Mr. William Hayes, seconded hy Mr. J. T. Smith. Thanks are also due to Mr. G. Marshall (secretary), Mr. F. Walker (ex-secretary), and Mr. C. Broadhurst (referee), for the very able manner in which they conducted such an en- joyable competition.
